Cycle 5 (Term 1: Weeks 9-10) Programming Fundamentals

1.21 Development approaches

Syllabus
Compare the execution of the Waterfall and Agile project management models as applied to software development.

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Compare the Waterfall and Agile project management models as applied to software development.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Define the Waterfall and Agile project management models.
  • Understand the differences between the Waterfall and Agile project management models.
  • Explain the advantages and disadvantages of each model.
  • Identify the types of projects that are suitable for each model.

  Content

Waterfall Model

Sequential Phases: The Waterfall model follows a linear and sequential approach where the project is divided into distinct phases. Each phase depends on the deliverables of the previous one and corresponds to a specialisation of tasks.

Documentation: There is a heavy emphasis on documentation at each phase. Before proceeding to the next phase, documentation must be completed and approved, ensuring that each stage's requirements are thoroughly understood and met.

Planning and Predictability: Detailed planning is crucial to the Waterfall model. The scope, budget, timeline, resources, and testing plans are defined early in the project. This approach aims for predictability and minimal changes during the project lifecycle.

Testing: In the Waterfall model, testing is a distinct phase that occurs after development is completed. Any errors discovered during testing can lead to significant revisions in previous work.

Client Involvement: Client involvement is generally limited to the requirements phase and final approval. After the project has moved beyond the initial stages, changes can be challenging to implement and often require returning to the drawing board.

 

The waterfall model is particularly suited to software development, where all requirements can be defined and understood before planning and design commence. It is most advantageous for custom large-scale systems that have precise specifications. Most errors occur in the requirements definition and formation of the software's specifications, with results showing that more than half of all errors occur at this stage. Correcting mistakes becomes increasingly expensive as the development cycle progresses.

 

Agile Model

Iterative Development: Unlike Waterfall, Agile adopts an iterative and incremental approach. Development is conducted in cycles (sprints), allowing for frequent reassessment and adaptation of plans. This approach facilitates flexibility in responding to changes.

The stages in an agile model are generally shorter than those in a waterfall model. These stages include:

  1. Defining and understanding
  2. Planning, designing and implementing
  3. Testing and evaluation
  4. Release a working version
  5. Define new requirements and repeat from the 2nd stage

Continuous Collaboration: Agile emphasises constant collaboration among team members and with stakeholders. Daily stand-ups, sprint reviews, and retrospectives are standard practices that encourage ongoing communication and adjustment.

Adaptability: Agile is highly adaptive, allowing for project scope and requirements changes even late in the development process. This flexibility is seen as a strength, enabling the delivery of a product that better meets the user's needs.

Testing: In Agile, testing is integrated throughout the development process. Continuous integration and delivery practices ensure that testing is ongoing, allowing for the early detection of issues and smoother iterations.

Client Involvement: Clients or end-users are significantly more involved throughout the project. Their feedback is incorporated into each iteration, ensuring the final product is closely aligned with their expectations and needs.

 

The agile model is a recently emerged development method responding to software development projects' "ad-hoc" reality. It emphasises the team developing the system rather than the predefined structured steps. The agile model removes the need for detailed requirements and complex design documentation; rather, it encourages cooperation, communication, and teamwork between the developers and the client. It is well suited to web-based software development and software that requires regular modification as it evolves and updates.

Small teams of developers are typically used, not much more than half a dozen developers. Small teams can share ideas better and work on solutions together. Larger teams tend to break into smaller groups. For the agile model to succeed, everyone must be an equal member with a clear shared purpose. Team members are often multi-skilled to contribute to multiple development activities.

The agile model allows a working version of the software to be released in a shorter amount of time. Basic functionality should be the initial version so the software can be released immediately. Ongoing interactions between the team and the client allow the solution to be refined throughout development. New versions are regularly released, adding the next most important features or adapting to changing specifications.

 

Comparing the Models

Aspect Waterfall Model Agile Model
Development Approach Linear and sequential approach Iterative and incremental approach
Phases Divided into distinct, sequential phases Shorter stages with cycles (sprints)
Documentation Heavy emphasis on documentation at each phase Emphasis on collaboration over extensive documentation
Planning and Predictability Detailed planning early in the project for predictability Adaptive planning, allows for changes even late in the process
Testing Testing as a distinct phase after development completion Testing integrated throughout the development process
Client Involvement Limited to requirements phase and final approval Continuous involvement; client feedback incorporated iteratively
Flexibility to Changes Changes challenging to implement once project progresses Highly adaptive, accommodates changes throughout
Team Size Can accommodate larger teams Typically involves smaller, cross-functional teams
Development Speed Slower due to sequential nature Faster release of working versions, enabling quick iterations
Suitability Suited for well-defined, large-scale projects with clear specifications Suited for projects with changing requirements and regular modifications
Error Handling Errors may be expensive to correct as the cycle progresses Early detection of issues with ongoing testing for smoother iterations
Client Interaction Limited interaction after initial stages Continuous collaboration with ongoing client feedback
Ideal Project Types Custom large-scale systems with precise specifications Web-based development, projects requiring regular modifications

 

Scenario 1: Construction Project

  • Description: A company is developing a large-scale construction project management software that requires strict regulatory compliance and integration with legacy systems. The requirements are well-defined, and the project scope is clear, with no expected changes.
  • Why Waterfall: The Waterfall model is ideal for this scenario due to the project's complexity and the need for extensive documentation and planning. Each phase (requirements, design, implementation, etc.) can be meticulously executed with approvals at every stage, ensuring compliance and compatibility. The sequential nature of Waterfall fits projects where changes are costly, and requirements are not expected to change.

 

Scenario 2: E-Commerce Mobile Application

  • Description: A startup wants to develop an e-commerce mobile application to enter the market quickly. The initial release will be followed by regular updates based on user feedback and emerging market trends.
  • Why Agile: Agile is suitable for this scenario because it allows the project to adapt rapidly to changing requirements and user feedback. The iterative development process enables the team to release a minimum viable product (MVP) quickly and refine it over time based on actual user interactions. Agile facilitates continuous improvement and can effectively respond to competitors and market demands.

Understanding and Programming in OOP

2.1 The Object Oriented Paradigm

Syllabus
Compare procedural programming with OOP

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Explore and comprehend the fundamental principles of the object-oriented programming paradigm, including classes, objects, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction and encapsulation

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Define key OOP concepts
  • Explain the advantages of using OOP
  • Demonstrate an understanding of classes and objects
  • Apply OOP principles to create simple applications
  • Identify practical applications of OOP principles

  Content

 The Object-Oriented Paradigm

Object-oriented programming (OOP) is a programming paradigm that structures computer code using the concept of objects, making the code easier to understand and manage. Instead of just writing lines of instructions one after the other (procedural programming), we organise our code into special groups called classes. Think of classes as templates or blueprints for creating specific types of objects.

An object is a bit like a playable character in a multiplayer video game.

All players have data (attributes) that are associated with them:

  • Gamertag
  • Position
  • Health Stats
  • Attack Stats
  • Defence Stats

Players also have actions (methods) to handle specific tasks that affect their own attributes or the attributes of other players:

  • Move up/down/left/right
  • Heal
  • Deal damage
  • Block attack

Players can also spawn (instantiation) multiple times depending on how many users join the game, all with the same set of methods and attributes.

The game programmer can also stop people from cheating in the game by seeing the current coordinate position of all players. The programmer achieves this by keeping the position attribute private to the player themselves (encapsulation), so that players can't access another player's position.

We may also want different subtypes of players (inheritance), like heroes, villains, healers, and demons.

Overall, OOP helps us keep things organised and makes it easier to reuse and fix our code. It's a bit like building with Lego blocks – you have different pieces that fit together to create something bigger (your program).

A note on terminology between Procedural Programming and Object Oriented Programming. In classes,

  • Variables are called Attributes
  • Functions/Procedures are called Methods

 

 Procedural Programming vs Object-Oriented Programming

The main difference between procedural programming and object-oriented programming is in their fundamental approach to organising code and data.

In procedural programming, the code is organised around procedures or functions, with a focus on the sequential execution of these procedures to achieve a task. Data is often global and can be accessed from anywhere in the program, leading to potential issues with data integrity and code maintenance.

On the other hand, object-oriented programming (OOP) organises code around objects, which encapsulate both data and behaviour. Objects are instances of classes, which serve as blueprints defining the structure and behaviour of objects. OOP emphasises modularity, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism, allowing for more organised, reusable, and easier-to-maintain code compared to procedural programming.

In summary, procedural programming revolves around functions or procedures, while object-oriented programming revolves around objects and classes.

Procedural-Oriented Programming (POP) Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)

It is a top-down approach

 It is a bottom-up approach

The program is divided into functions

 The program is divided into objects

Doesn't use Access Modifiers

Makes use of Access Modifiers 'public', 'private', 'protected'

It is less secure

 It is more secure

Data can move freely from function to function within programs

 The object can move freely within member functions

It does not support inheritance

 It supports inheritance

Syllabus
Apply the key features of an object-oriented programming (OOP) language Including:
- classes

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Gain a deep understanding of object classes and encapsulation, two foundational principles of object-oriented programming, and learn how to effectively apply these concepts in software development

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Define objects, classes and encapsulation
  • Explain the characteristics of objects and classes
  • Implement classes in a programming environment
  • Demonstrate the use of encapsulation
  • Apply encapsulation to ensure data integrity
  • Identify practical applications of object classes and encapsulation

  Content

In 2.1, The Object-Oriented Paradigm, we provided a high-level overview of the main concepts of object-oriented programming. In module 2.2, we will discuss these concepts in more detail.

Classes

A class is like a blueprint or template for creating objects. It defines the properties (attributes) and behaviours (methods) that objects of that class will have. Think of a class as a recipe for creating objects. It encapsulates data (see encapsulation heading below) for the object and provides methods to operate on that data.

Here's how we construct a generic Person class in Python:

Class Name

In Python, a class is defined using the class Keyword followed by the class name. It is a standard programming convention to capitalise the first letter of a class name (e.g. Person, Animal, Vehicle).

Attributes

After defining a class, we need to list the attributes that a Person should have. Since the value of these attributes varies from person to person, we will initially set each of these to None.

Constructor Method

We now need to add a constructor method that builds an object out of the Person class.

A constructor in Python is a special method that gets called automatically when a new object of a class is created. It is used to initialise the object's state, using the arguments to pass values specific to the person being created into our previously empty attributes. In Python, the constructor method is named __init__. It allows you to perform any necessary setup operations when creating a new instance of a class.

Note: In Python, self is a reference to the current instance of a class. It's used inside methods to access the attributes and other methods of the containing class. For example, self.firstName refers to the firstName attribute defined above the constructor method whereas firstName inside the constructor refers to the method's parameter.

Methods

Finally, we can add in the methods that perform actions based on the attributes.

Methods in Python are functions defined within a class. They are used to define the behavior of objects created from that class. Methods can access and modify the attributes (data) of an object and perform actions related to that object.

Objects

An object is an instance of a class. It is created using the blueprint provided by the class (this is called instantiation). Each object has its own set of properties and can perform actions defined by the class.

In Python, you instantiate an object by calling the class name followed by parentheses containing any arguments required by the class's constructor (the __init__ method). This process creates a new instance of the class, which is an object with its own set of attributes and methods.

In the context of our Person class, we can create multiple Person objects, each representing a different person with unique attributes. We can also access the components of our instantiated class (i.e. accessing the object's attributes and using the object's methods).

Output:

John Smith
Phone No: 0432783491
Email: johnsmith@email.com
Is not an adult
Is an adult

 

Encapsulation

Encapsulation is one of the fundamental principles of object-oriented programming (OOP).

Encapsulation allows us to hide the attributes (data) within a class and makes them available only through well-defined interface methods (getter and setter methods). The only way to access and modify hidden attributes are through these interface methods. This helps in maintaining consistency and security for the data in an object.

We can also hide certain methods which are only used from within the class itself and don't need to be accessed by other objects or the rest of the program.

Attributes and methods can be set to three different visibility modifiers:

  • Public (default) - Accessible inside or outside the class.
  • Protected _ - Accessible within the class or its sub-classes
  • Private __ - Accessible only within the class.

 

The key ideas behind the use of encapsulation are:

  1. Data Hiding: Encapsulation allows you to hide the internal state of an object from outside interference. This means that the implementation details of the class are hidden as private and cannot be accessed directly from outside the class.

  2. Access Control: Encapsulation enables you to control access to the attributes of a class. By defining access modifiers like public, private, and protected, you can specify which parts of the class are accessible from outside and which are not.

  3. Abstraction: Encapsulation provides a way to abstract the implementation details of a class. It allows you to focus on what an object does rather than how it does it, promoting a clear separation between the interface and implementation.

Encapsulation helps in achieving modularity, reusability, and maintainability of code by reducing dependencies and preventing unintended modifications to the internal state of objects.

 

In Python, encapsulation can be achieved by using private attributes and methods, indicated by prefixing them with a double underscore __.

Consider our example class Person. Using encapsulation, we can ensure that the age attribute is never set to a value less than or equal to 0 by first making it private using a two underscore (__) prefix.

Since the __age attribute is now hidden from everything outside the Person class in our program, we must write a getter method (getAge()) and setter method (setAge()) for the __age attribute.

Getter and setter methods are like guards for the information inside an object. They control how you can see and change that information (i.e. other objects cannot directly access the __age attribute, they can only use the getter and setter methods that the programmer provides).

Getter Method: getAge()

  • Getter methods are used to access the value of a private attribute from outside the class. In this program, getAge() is a getter method that allows retrieving the value of the private attribute __age.
  • It returns the value of __age.

Setter Method: setAge()

  • Setter methods are used to modify the value of a private attribute from outside the class, usually with some validation.
  • In this program, setAge(age) is a setter method that sets the value of the private attribute __age.
  • Before setting the age, it checks whether the input age is non-negative (greater than 0). If it's not, it prints a message indicating that the age cannot be less than or equal to 0 (the attribute remains as None).
  • If the input age is valid, it sets the value of __age to the input value.

Constructor:

  • Since we now have a setter method (setAge()) that guards the __age attribute against unwanted inputs, we can replace the variable assignment self.__age = age in the constructor with self.setAge().

Below, we instantiate the Person class but the __age attribute is now private instead of public.

When accessing and printing the values of the firstName and address attributes, we are not given any errors because they are public and easily accessible to everything in our program.

However, if try to access and print the value of the private __age attribute, we are given an error which says that the program cannot find the attribute __age (which is what we want since we've hidden that attribute from everything outside the Person object).

Output:

John
5 Pennant Hills Road

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/Users/martin/Desktop/Python OOP/Person.py", line 60, in <module>
    print(person1.__age)
AttributeError: 'Person' object has no attribute '__age'

 

Since the __age attribute is private, we must use getAge() to access its value. We don't get an error unlike before.

Output:

John
5 Pennant Hills Road
17

 

If we want to change the value of the __age attribute, we must use setAge() method instead of directly accessing the attribute.

Output:

Is not an adult
Is an adult

 

If we try to enter an invalid age, the __age attribute will not change its value because it is guarded by the checks in the setAge() method.

Output:

Can't have an age <= 0!
17

2.2.2 OOP Features: Inheritance

Syllabus
Apply the key features of an object-oriented programming (OOP) language Including:
- inheritance

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Learn and apply the concept of inheritance in object-oriented programming to effectively reuse and extend existing code

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Define inheritance
  • Explain the benefits of using inheritance
  • Implement single inheritance in a programming environment
  • Use inherited methods
  • Demonstrate the use of the super() function
  • Identify real-world applications of inheritance

  Content

Please complete the EdStem Activities: Objects, Classes & Encapsulation, and then Multi-file Programs BEFORE continuing further. If you do not complete these, you will be lost following the walkthrough below.

Inheritance

Inheritance is a key concept in object-oriented programming (OOP) that allows classes to inherit attributes and methods from other classes. This enables the creation of a hierarchical structure of classes, where child classes can reuse and extend the functionality of their parent class.

When a class inherits from another class, it automatically gains access to all the attributes and methods that are defined in the parent class. This means that the child class can use and manipulate the data and behaviours defined in the parent class without redefining them.

Inheritance in OOP can be understood as an "is-a" relationship, which represents a form of classification or categorisation. In this context, the child class is said to be a more specialised version of the parent class.

Person Class

Recall the Person class in Person.py from the end of the EdStem Activity: Multi-file Programs.

Please take a look at the finished Person.py code as a reference only after attempting the EdStem Activities!

Sample Answer for Person.py

 

Student Class

We can create a new Student class as a child class of Person (since Student is a type of Person).

We will do this in a new file called Student.py.

Your folder structure should now look like this:

 

In Student.py, we will need to import the Person class from Person.py at the top of the file.

The Student class then defines its parent class Person in brackets () next to the class name.

The Student class inherits everything (attributes and methods) that the Person class has, plus a few extra things specific to a student:

  • studentId (specific identifier for a student in a school)
  • subjects (a list of HSC subjects that a student takes)

We now need a constructor method __init__() so that we can instantiate the Student class into objects.

This constructor method's parameters should have the same parameters as the Person class's constructor method.

  • firstName, lastName, age, address, phoneNo, email

The constructor method's parameters should also have the additional attributes that were introduced in the Person class.

  • studentId

The reason why we don't handle subjects in the constructor method because we want to initially leave it as an empty list. We can use setter methods later to add/remove subjects after being instantiated as an object.

In Python, we can use super() to access the public/protected methods and attributes from the parent class.

In the Student class's constructor, we don't want to call each setter method again for the attributes that are inherited from the Person class.

Using super(), any attributes that are directly inherited from the Person class (firstName, lastName, age, address, phoneNo, email) can set their values by simply re-using the Person class's constructor.

  • super().__init__(firstName, lastName, age, address, phoneNo, email)

Any new attributes are then set after calling the Person class's constructor.

  • self.setStudentId(studentId)

We then implement the getter and setter methods (just as we did for the Person class's attributes).

  • getStudentId
  • getSubjects
  • setStudentId
  • addSubject - Adds the string name of a subject in the subjects list
  • removeSubject - Removes the string name of a subject in the subjects list

Plus any other methods that define the behaviours of the Student class.

  • numberOfUnits

In main.py, to use the Student class we need to import it using

  • from classes.Student import Student

We can then instantiate a Student object before adding each subject that the student does (addSubject()).

Like any other object, we can access its public methods (getStudentId(), getSubjects(), numberOfUnits()).

Output:

ID: 39473
Subjects: ['Maths', 'English', 'Biology', 'Physics', 'Chemistry', 'Modern History', 'Legal Studies']
Units: 14

 

The benefit of inheritance is that we can also access the parent class's methods (in this case, the Student class can access the public methods in the Person class).

Output:

May Smith
Phone No: 0432123456
Email: msmith@email.com
Is not an adult

2.2.3 OOP Features: Polymorphism

Syllabus
Apply the key features of an object-oriented programming (OOP) language Including:
- polymorphism

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand and apply concepts of inheritance and polymorphism in object-oriented programming.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Define polymorphism
  • Understand the relationship between inheritance and polymorphsim
  • Use inheritance and polymorphism in a programming environment
  • Identify practical applications of inheritance and polymorphism

  Content

Please complete the EdStem Activity: Inheritance BEFORE continuing further.

Inheritance & Polymorphism

Recall the definition of inheritance from module 2.2.2 OOP Features: Inheritance.

"Inheritance is a key concept in object-oriented programming (OOP) that allows classes to inherit attributes and methods from other classes. This enables the creation of a hierarchical structure of classes, where child classes can reuse and extend the functionality of their parent class"

 

But what if we wanted a method (that is inherited from the parent class) to do something different in the child class?

For example:

  • All animals can make a sound. However, not all animals make the same sound.

We can achieve this through polymorphism!

 

In object-oriented programming (OOP), inheritance and polymorphism are closely related concepts, often used together to promote code reuse, modularity, and extensibility. The relationship between inheritance and polymorphism lies in the fact that inheritance enables polymorphism.

 

Polymorphism

Polymorphism is a key concept in object-oriented programming (OOP) that allows for classes of objects to behave in different ways (depending on the context) without changing the interface in which they are used (i.e. the way in which we interact with the object).

To put it simply, polymorphism allows us to perform a single action in different ways.

Note: The interface of a class is simply defined as the method signatures in the class (the method names and associated parameters)

 

Method Overriding

In Python, polymorphism is achieved through a technique called Method Overriding. Method overriding is where an inherited method in a child class is declared again with the same name and parameters, but operates in a different way than the same method in the parent class.

Consider a parent class called Animal, where its interface consists of the methods:

  • getName()
  • setName()
  • make_sound()
  • eat()

All animals can make a sound through the make_sound() method and can eat through the eat() method.

 

However, we would want child classes like Dog and Cat to make different sounds when using the method make_sound() (but the way they eat remains the same).

Consider the child classes Dog and Cat.

 

The Dog child class uses method overriding to change the output of the make_sound() method to "Woof! Woof!" to suit the context of the class.

Similarly, the Cat child class uses method overriding to change the output of the make_sound() method to "Meow! Meow!" to suit the context of the class.

 

In both the Dog and Cat child classes, the make_sound() method is defined in the same way as the Animal parent class using def make_sound(self):, but the code inside of the method behaves differently.

 

We now demonstrate the use of polymorphism when these classes are instantiated as interactable objects.

Output:

Alex says generic animal sound
Max says Woof! Woof!
Tom says Meow! Meow!
Alex is eating
Max is eating
Tom is eating

 

Notice how we can interact with the objects belonging to the Animal class (and its subclasses) by using the same make_sound() method, but the subclasses behave differently from the Animal parent class.

Additionally, notice how the behaviour in the eat() method remains the same since eat() was not overridden in the Dog or Cat child classes.

2.2.4 OOP Features: Generalisation & Abstraction

Syllabus
Apply the key features of an object-oriented programming (OOP) language Including:
- generalisation
- abstraction

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand and apply the concepts of abstraction and generalisation in object-oriented programming to design more efficient and maintainable code

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Define Abstraction and Generalisation
  • Explain the purpose of abstraction in OOP
  • Implement abstracting using abstract classes and methods
  • Understand generalisation and its role in creating class hierarchies
  • Apply generalisation to design a class structure
  • Identify real-world applications of abstraction and generalisation

  Content

Please complete the EdStem Activity: Polymorphism BEFORE continuing further. 

Generalisation

Generalisation revolves around the concept of reusability in object oriented programming.

The process of generalisation aims to reduce copied code and improve maintainability by finding common traits among various specific classes and creating a general class from these traits.

 

Example of Generalising Classes

We achieve generalisation by extracting the essential characteristics (attributes and methods) that are shared between related or similar classes. These common characteristics then form the generalised parent class of those classes (which are now child classes).

Consider two separate classes called FullTimeEmployee and PartTimeEmployee.

Both types of employees have a name, a job title and a list of tasks. Full-time employees have a yearly salary, which is paid on a monthly basis. Part-time employees have a set number of working hours per week and are paid on an hourly rate.

Looking at the FullTimeEmployee and PartTimeEmployee classes, we can find common characteristics.

Both classes have the same:

  • attributes __name, __title and __tasks
  • methods getName(), getTitle(), getTasks(), setName(), setTitle(), addTask() and removeTask()

Additionally, the first 3 lines of the printInfo() method are the same between the classes.

 

Using these common characteristics, let us create a generalised parent class called Employee that will contain the attributes and methods that ALL types of employees should have.

To complete the generalisation process, we must modify the FullTimeEmployee and PartTimeEmployee classes so that they are child classes that inherit from the Employee parent class.

The common attributes and methods that were placed in the Employee parent class can now be removed from the FullTimeEmployee and PartTimeEmployee classes since these are inherited from the Employee class.

Notice how the FullTimeEmployee and PartTimeEmployee classes are substantially shorter than before, only containing the attributes and methods that are specific to the type of employee with common characteristics placed out of sight in the Employee parent class.

  • FullTimeEmployee contains the attributes and methods that deal with a salary
  • PartTimeEmployee contains the attributes and methods that deal with an hourly rate
  • Employee contains the attributes and methods that all types employees should have (name, job title and tasks)

A benefit of having common characteristics contained in a single class is that it allows us to make modifications to these characteristics which will apply to all child classes without the need to manually make the same modification to multiple classes.

 

Use of Polymorphism in printInfo()

The only difference in the printInfo() method between the FullTimeEmployee and PartTimeEmployee classes was the last print() statement which either showed the employee's salary or hourly rate.

  • The first three print() statements which displayed the employee's name, title and tasks have been placed in the printInfo() method of the Employee parent class.
  • The last print() statement has remained in the now overridden printInfo() method of the FullTimeEmployee and PartTimeEmployee classes, where the printInfo() method of the Employee parent class is called using super().printInfo() before running the last print() statement to show either the salary or hourly rate depending on the child class.

 

The Need for Abstraction

Currently, the Employee parent class guarantees that all types employees must have a name, a job title and a list of tasks. However, it does NOT guarantee that all types employees must be paid. In other words, nothing is preventing the programmer from accidentally (or on purpose) omitting the calculate_pay() method from a child class of Employee.

We can enforce that all Employees must have a calculate_pay() method by using ABSTRACTION.

 

Abstraction

Abstraction revolves around the concept of hiding implementation details and focusing on the essential features of a class. This benefits the programmer, helping to manage complexity by allowing them to deal with ideas rather than specifics.

In Python and many other object oriented programming languages we are able to declare classes and methods as 'abstract'.

  • For a class this means it cannot be instantiated, as such, the only way to access its attributes and methods is to create a subclass which can inherit these features which can then be used.
  • For an abstract method, this means that the implementation is not defined in the method, but will rather be defined in subclasses.

For example, consider a set of different characters in a video game.

  • We know at a minimum that all characters in this video game must move, but we don't know how each type of character will move. Some characters might walk normally on the ground, some might be able to fly and some might be able to dig underground.
  • Using abstraction, we can have an unimplemented move() method inside a generalised character class which hides the complex details of how different characters will move; leaving each type of character to implement their own move() method in each child class.

 

Example of Abstraction

We achieve generalisation by using the Abstract Base Classes (ABC) library which is a Python standard library. This library is imported at the top of the Python file by using:

  • from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

Consider the generalised Employee parent class from before.

The Employee class will need to abstracted for two reasons.

  1. To prevent the Employee class itself from being instantiated into an object. We need all employee objects to be instantiated from specific types of employees only (the child classes of Employee).
  2. To ensure that all child classes of Employee have a calculate_pay() method. We need all employee objects to have this method.

 

First, we need to import the Abstract Base Classes (ABC) library and define the Employee class as an abstract class.

  • This tells the Python interpreter that the Employee class cannot be instantiated into an object; it can only be inherited from.

 

Second, we need to add the calculate_pay() method as an abstract method using @abstractmethod tag above the method's definition and using the keyword pass inside the method's implementation.

  • This tells the Python interpreter that any class that inherits from Employee must have an implemented calculate_pay() method.

Now consider a new type of employee called InternEmployee which is a child class of the Employee class.

Notice how the calculate_pay() method is missing from the InternEmployee class. If we tried to instantiate this class as it is, then we will be met with the following error message.

Output:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/Users/martin/Desktop/Python OOP/main.py", line 3, in <module>
    employee = Employee("Martin Madrid", "Software Engineer", "UNSW")
TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Employee with abstract method calculate_pay

 

By adding the calculate_pay() abstract method in the Employee parent class, it prevents the InternEmployee child class from being instantiated into an object without the calculate_pay() method.

To fix this error, we need to implement the calculate_pay() method in the InternEmployee class like so.

By implementing all abstract methods in the Employee parent class, we can now instantiate the InternEmployee child class.

Output:

Employee Name: Martin Madrid
Title: Software Engineer
Current Tasks: ['Task 1', 'Task 2']
University: UNSW
Allowance: $20000

2.3 Represent a System (Diagrams)

Syllabus
Use data flow diagrams, structure charts and class diagrams to represent a system

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand and apply data flow diagrams, structure charts and class diagrams in software design and analysis

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Create and interpret data flow diagrams, structure charts and class diagrams to represent a system
  • Apply diagrams to real-world scenarios

  Content

In system analysis and design, diagrams play a crucial role in visualising and understanding the structure, processes, and interactions within a system. Different types of diagrams focus on specific aspects, helping developers, analysts, and stakeholders to communicate ideas and create effective designs.

 

Class Diagrams 

The Object Oriented Paradigm is "design first" as we need to design our objects and relationships first before we begin programming so that we have a clear outline of how to structure our program. Class diagrams aid us in the designing process helping to model our objects and their relationships so we can reference the diagram as we implement a system.

 

Class diagrams are a type of diagram defined in the Unifed Modeling Language (UML), which is a standard used to visualise the design of a system. They describe the structure of a system, showing the classes in a system, their attributes, methods and the relationships between classes.

 

The basic building blocks of a class diagrams are Classes, which are represented as a rectangle, divided into three parts:

  • The class' name
  • Attributes of the class, with the type of the attribute is specified with a colon and then the type.
  • Methods that the class implements, with the parameters in parenthesis and then the return type specified after a colon

 

In a class diagram we can create many classes and then represent their structure by specifying relationships between them. These may include:

Type Use
 Example
Inheritance Represents a relationship between a child class and a parent class
Relationship

Models the relationship where a class can use or own objects from another class

Multiplicities specify the number of instances of one class that can be associated with one instance of another class.

Aside: Relationships

Relationships are a powerful type of connection we can use between classes to add functionality to a program as it allows a class to "use" or "own" objects from another class.

One example of this is where a Student studies a Subject. The Subject class is able to store a List of Students that study the Subject, thus forming the relationship between the two classes. Here's how we can model this example in a class diagram:

Take note how Subject contains a list of Students, this list stores the objects of Students themselves. With this in mind, let's have a look at what this will look like in Python.

First, consider the Student class.

Following the design specified in the class diagram, the Student class contains three attributes: student_id, first_name and last_name, as well as the method print_details() to get the student's info. Now let's have a look at Subject, to see how the relationship is implemented.

Notice how we have the list of Students as per the class diagram, when enroll_student() is called the list is appended to with the Student object. As we are storing the students in a list within the subject we have formed the relationship between them.

Now that we have two complete classes we can instantiate objects and add Students to Classes. Consider this mainline.

 

Here, we instantiate two Student objects as well as one Subject and then enroll the students in the subject, adding them to the list attribute inside the Subject. Then when we call the print_all_students() method we loop through each student and call the Student class' print_details() method. Here is the output produced for reference:

Students enrolled in Software Engineering:
Student ID: 001
Name: Viraj Patel
Student ID: 002
Name: Vedant Upmanyue

Cycle 8 (Term 2: Weeks 5-6) OOP

2.4 Collaborative Code Development

Syllabus
Outline the features of OOP that support collaborative code development including:
- consistency
- code commenting
- version control
- feedback

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand and explain how Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) features support collaborative code development, focusing on consistency, code commenting, version control, and feedback mechanisms.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Explain how OOP features like modularity, naming conventions, design patterns, and comments contribute to consistency and readability in collaborative development.
  • Describe the role of version control systems in managing code changes and the importance of code reviews, automated testing, and CI/CD pipelines in maintaining high code quality.

  Content

Collaborative code development is a practice where multiple developers work together on a shared codebase to build, maintain, and enhance software projects. 

 

Consistency

  1. Modularity and Encapsulation: OOP encourages the use of classes and objects to represent real-world entities, promoting a consistent and organised structure within the codebase. By defining clear interfaces and encapsulating data and behaviour within classes, developers can maintain a standardised approach across different modules and components of the software. Review this content here: 2.2.1 OOP Features: Objects, Classes & Encapsulation

  2. Standard Naming Conventions: OOP encourages the use of consistent naming conventions for classes, methods, and variables. This practice ensures that the code is readable and understandable by all team members, reducing confusion and enhancing collaboration.

  3. Design Patterns: Using established design patterns (e.g., Facade) ensures a uniform approach to solving common problems, making the codebase predictable and easier to understand and maintain. Review the content for the Facade pattern here: 2.5 Code Design

  4. Reusable Components: Classes and objects can be reused across different parts of the codebase. This reuse promotes consistency in code behaviour and reduces duplication of code.

 

Code Commenting

  1. Documentation Comments: Comments written within the code itself allows developers to document the overall purpose, functionality, and usage of classes and their methods. Properly commented code enhances readability and understanding, facilitating collaboration among team members who may be working on different parts of the project.

  2. Inline Comments: These comments are placed within the code to explain complex logic, decisions, or unusual implementations. They help other developers understand the rationale behind specific code sections, facilitating easier maintenance and updates.

  3. TODO Comments: These comments highlight areas of the code that need further development, testing, or refactoring. They help keep track of pending tasks and ensure that important updates are not overlooked.

  4. Consistent Commenting Style: Adopting a consistent commenting style across the project ensures that all team members can easily read and interpret comments, enhancing overall code comprehension and reducing miscommunication.

 

Code Commenting Example

The example below demonstrates a Library system which uses different types of comments (documentation, inline, consistent, todo) throughout the code to improve readability.

 

Version Control

  1. Branching and Merging: Version Control Systems (VCS) allows developers to work on separate branches for different features or bug fixes. This isolation ensures that changes do not interfere with the main codebase until they are ready to be safely integrated. Merging branches enables the combination of these changes into the main codebase, facilitating collaborative development. Branches with modified code need to be tested for errors first before being merged into the main codebase. This is so that the main codebase always remains as stable as possible.

  2. Commit History: Every change made to the code is recorded with a commit, which includes a message describing the change. The commit messages form a history that provides a detailed record of what was changed, who made the change, and why it was made, making it easier to track progress and understand the evolution of the codebase.

  3. Conflict Resolution: When multiple developers work on the same code, conflicts can arise. VCS tools provide mechanisms to detect, highlight, and resolve these conflicts, ensuring that the final code is coherent and integrates contributions from all team members.

  4. Collaboration Platforms: Platforms like GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket offer additional collaborative features such as pull requests, code reviews, and issue tracking, which streamline the development process and enhance team coordination.

 

Version Control with Git

Git is a version control system (VCS), it allows us to track project changes and work together on a codebase in a team. Take a look at the video to learn how to use Git and how we can use GitHub to manage a repository.

For more information on these different collaboration platforms take a look back at: 1.2 Online collaboration tools.

 

Feedback

  1. Code Reviews: Programmers are generally biased towards their own code, thinking that they are correct despite being potentially flawed. A code review handles this bias by having someone other than the original programmer check the correctness the code. Peer reviews of code changes help identify potential issues, enforce coding standards, and share knowledge among team members. This collaborative practice improves code quality and fosters a culture of continuous improvement.

  2. Automated Testing: Unit tests, integration tests, and automated testing frameworks ensure that code changes do not introduce new bugs or regressions. Automated test results provide immediate feedback on the impact of changes, enabling developers to address issues promptly. Review this content here: 1.18 Test and evaluate.

  3. Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD): CI/CD pipelines automate the process of building, testing, and deploying code. They provide immediate feedback on the status of the codebase, ensuring that it remains in a deployable state and that issues are caught early in the development cycle.

Initial Clone of a Repository

  1. Use git clone <url> to clone the repository. Remember to replace the <url> with the link that is found under: Code (green button) > HTTPS (see screenshot below).

    Reason: We must be editing our code locally on Visual Studio Code, not using the online editor on GitHub.




 

 

 Using a Branch to Add Features

  1. Change the Visual Studio Code workspace to the folder that was created from cloning the repository. Use the command git pull origin main to update the local repository with any changes that may be on the GitHub repository.

    Reason: Ensures your local repository is synchronized with the remote repository to avoid conflicts.



  2. Then, create a new branch for your feature using this command git checkout -b <new-feature-branch>. Remember to replace <new-feature-branch> with the name of the feature that you are implementing (you come up with this name).

    Reason: Creating a new branch allows you to work on the new feature without affecting the main branch. 



  3. Now, implement the code for your new feature in your local environment, i.e., Visual Studio Code.



  4. After this, you may stage all the changes you've made to the code by running the command git add .

    Reason: Staging the changes prepares them to be committed. You can also add specific files instead of all changes.



  5. Commit the changes with a message through the command, git commit -m "Add feature X". Make sure you include an appropriate message with your commit that details the changes you made.

    Reason: Commit messages should be descriptive to provide context about the changes.



  6. Push the changes to the remote repository by using git push.

    At this stage you will likely be asked to login to GitHub if you have not already. For the first push we do to a new branch, there is be no corresponding branch on the GitHub repository so the push command will fail (see screenshot). So, just copy the command in the error, git push --set-upstream origin <branch-name>,  to push it for the first time, you only need to run this command once for a new branch.

    Reason: Pushing the changes uploads your branch to the remote repository, making it available for review and merging.



  7. Create a Pull Request and Merge on GitHub
        •    Copy the link that you received when running the git push command from the previous step. Paste it into your browser; it should be in the form https://github.com/<username>/<repository>/pull/new/<branch>
        •    Fill in a meaningful title and description for your pull request, then press the "Create pull request" button
        •    Review the changes, address any comments or feedback.
        •    Once approved, merge the pull request into the main branch.

    Reason: Merging via a pull request allows for code review and ensures that the main branch is always stable.




  8. Return to Visual Studio Code and checkout the main branch which you have just merged your changes to by using git checkout main

    Reason: Switches your working directory back to the main branch to incorporate the latest changes.



  9. Pull the latest changes from the main branch with the command git pull origin main

    Reason: Ensures your local main branch is up to date with the remote main branch, including the new feature you just merged.



  10. Repeat from Step 1 whenever you want to add a new feature into your program.

    Reason: To add a new feature into the codebase.

 

 

 

 

 

2.5 Code Design

Syllabus
Describe the process of design used to develop code in an OOP language including:
- task definition
- top-down and bottom-up
- facade pattern
- agility

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Students will understand the process of designing code in an OOP language, including task definition, top-down and bottom-up approaches, the facade pattern, and agility in development.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Students can define coding tasks, apply design approaches, implement the facade pattern, and adapt their code to changing requirements efficiently.

  Content

The process of designing software in an object-oriented programming (OOP) language is essential for creating systems that are clear, scalable, and easy to maintain. Effective design ensures that code meets user requirements while adhering to best practices. This process involves defining tasks, choosing appropriate design approaches such as top-down or bottom-up, implementing design patterns like the facade pattern, and adopting agile principles to accommodate change.

 

Code Design

The main advantage of object-oriented programming over imperative programming is its unique ability to create elegant and beautiful software through a design that is centred around the use of objects; rather than functions used in procedural programming.

Throughout the remainder of this unit, the aim is to emphasise good design practices of object-oriented code as we apply the principles you have learned to effectively create modular systems that are flexible, maintainable and reusable.

When it comes to code design, there is no clear right or wrong answer. There are many shades of grey, where design decisions aren't clear cut. Good programming skill doesn't matter if you don't have good design. Designing elegant OOP software is an art.

Task Definition

A task definition (or problem statement) is a concise and clear description of a specific issue or challenge. It acts as a foundational element in the problem-solving process by clearly articulating what needs to be addressed. A well-crafted task definition should be focused, precise, and actionable, enabling individuals or teams to remain aligned on the objective and work collaboratively toward a solution.

Key Characteristics of a Good Task Definition

  1. Clarity: The problem should be easy to understand and free from jargon.
  2. Focus: It should highlight the core issue without unnecessary details.
  3. Importance: The statement should explain why solving the problem matters, emphasizing its significance.
  4. Impact: Identifies who or what is affected by the issue.
  5. Stimulates Creativity: Inspires innovative and critical thinking to develop effective solutions.

Top-Down and Bottom-Up

The Top-Down and Bottom-Up design methodologies represent two different approaches to system development.

  • Top-Down Design is an approach where the system is broken down into smaller components starting from the highest level.
    • In OOP, we would start by creating high-level generalised classes before creating lower-level child classes that have more specific responsibilities.
    • e.g. In a game, we may start by creating a generalised Character class before creating more specific child classes such as Knight and Witch.
  • Bottom-Up Design is an approach where the system is built starting from the lowest level components.
    • In OOP, we would start by creating low-level classes with specific responsibilities before generalising into higher-level parent classes.
    • e.g. In a game, we may start by creating the Knight and Witch classes before creating more a generalised Character class.

Façade Pattern

In software design, there are many established design approaches that are used as a template for handling common design problems. One such problem is having to deal with complexity of our object-oriented code. The solution is to create a simplified interface (facade) to hide the complexity of underlying classes in a way that allows people who are unfamiliar with the code (e.g. the client) to use the software.

The Facade Pattern is a design approach that provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem. It is particularly useful when you have a program with multiple interdependent classes, and you want to make it easier to use by providing a single interface to interact with that system.

Imagine your computer as one of these complex systems. The facade in this scenario is your keyboard, mouse and screen which offer you a method to control and use your computer whilst hiding the complexity and millions of operations going on behind the screen to provide you with a user friendly method to interact with the systems.

Example:

Consider a home entertainment system with:

  • A DVD Player
  • A Projector
  • Lights
  • A Sound System

To use the Facade Pattern in the design of this system, we can provide a simple interface class called RemoteControlFacade to interact with the components of the home theatre without knowing how to use each of those individual components.

The attributes of the RemoteControlFacade class contains the objects that make up the home theatre.

The methods of the RemoteControlFacade class then call the methods of those objects (dim(), on(), set_input(), set_volume(), etc).

We can then use the interface methods in the RemoteControlFacade to start and end a movie without needing to know how to use the DVDPlayer, Projector, Lights or SoundSystem classes. The client only needs to know how to use the facade interface.

Output:

Get ready to watch a movie...
Lights dimmed to 10%.
Projector is on.
Projector input set to DVD.
Sound system is on.
Sound system volume set to 5.
DVD Player is on.
Playing movie 'Imitation Game'.
Shutting movie theater down...
DVD Player is off.
Sound system is off.
Projector is off.
Lights dimmed to 100%.

 

Agility

When designing object-oriented code, it is important to structure classes in a way that allows for easy and efficient modification.

The agility of a program is described as its ability to adapt to unspecified or changing needs of the client.

This adaptability is crucial in modern software development, where requirements can evolve rapidly.

If adding a feature requires a large number of classes to be modified, then:

  • the update will take a long amount of time
  • the large number of modifications will likely cause existing features to fail

This is a sign of poorly designed OOP code.

However, if the same feature can be added by modifying a small number of classes, then:

  • the update will take a short amount of time
  • the small number of modifications will not largely affect existing features

This is a sign of effectively designed OOP code.

Ideally, when we need to add new features into our object-oriented code, these changes should only be made in as few places as possible. If you need to make changes in many other places too, then program development will become much more complicated and expensive as a result because of poor agile design.

Example:

Consider a video game that has to be frequently updated to receive new characters. If we have a generalised character class that contains the common attributes and behaviours across all characters in the game (e.g. moving, attacking, defending), then any modifications that add any new characters into the game will mainly require the addition of a single new child class and its specialised behaviours. The more changes that are required outside of the new child class, the less agile the object-oriented code becomes.

2.6 Message passing

Syllabus
Investigate how OOP languages handle message-passing between objects

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand how object-oriented programming (OOP) languages handle message passing between objects to facilitate communication and interaction in software systems.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Explain the concept of message passing in OOP and its role in enabling object interactions within software systems.
  • Demonstrate how to implement message passing between objects in an OOP language, using methods and parameters to simulate real-world interactions.

  Content

In Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), objects are the fundamental building blocks of a program. These objects communicate with each other to perform tasks, much like how individuals exchange information in real-life interactions. This communication is achieved through message-passing, where one object sends a request to another, prompting it to perform an action or share information.

Message-passing is more than just a way for objects to interact—it underpins core OOP principles like encapsulation, polymorphism, and abstraction, enabling flexible and modular software design. In this lesson, we will explore how different programming languages handle message-passing, the mechanics behind it, and its importance in creating scalable and maintainable systems.

 

Message Passing

Message passing in object-oriented programming (OOP) refers to the process by which objects can interact with each other. Objects interact with each other by sending a message that requests to run a method from a different object.

In other words, objects interact with each other by calling the methods of another object. For example, when Object A runs a method in Object B, then Object A is sending a message to Object B.

The process of message passing between objects works as follows:

  1. The sender object constructs a message that specifies: the name of the method and the required parameters to use that method.
  2. The message is sent to the receiving object to be processed.
  3. The receiving object then interprets the message. If the specified method exists and the message contains the all of the required parameters, then that method is run using those parameters.
  4. If the method returns a value, then it is sent back to the sender object.

Message passing allows different objects (the components of a program) to talk to each other without needing to know all the details about how the other works. This makes it easier for them to work together and simplifies the overall design. This approach promotes abstraction and encapsulation, where objects interact only through the well-defined interfaces of their methods, ensuring modularity and flexibility in software design.

 

Example of Message Passing

In Python, the concept of message passing involves any method that calls a method from another object.

Consider the Car class below which has a simple behavioural method called start() that starts the car's engine (represented using a print() statement for simplicity).

Now consider the Driver class. It has a behavioural method called drive(car) that takes in a car object as a parameter and runs that car object's start() method.

It is important to note that the drive(car) method does not need to know exactly how a car starts (i.e. putting the fuel in the engine, igniting the fuel, etc). The inner workings of the car are only being handled in the Car class itself, hidden away by its method interface. All the drive(car) method needs to know is that we can start a car object just by using its start() method.

The use of the drive(car) method through message passing is demonstrated in the mainline below. The car and driver objects are created before interacting with each other when the drive(car) method is called.

Output:

Kevin is sending a message to start the car.
BMW car is starting...

 

From the output, we can see that by calling the drive(car) method in the driver object, we also call the start() method in the given car object.

 

Note on Code Design

By using message passing, the drive(car) method is inherently designed to always require a car object (which makes sense because a driver needs a car in order to drive). If a driver is not given a car, then they cannot drive.

2.7 Code Effectiveness & Optimisation

Syllabus
Assess the effectiveness of programming code developed to implement an algorithm
Explain code optimisation in software engineering

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Students will be able to evaluate the effectiveness of programming code that implements a given algorithm, focusing on aspects such as correctness, efficiency, and readability

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Describe what the algorithm is designed to achieve and outline the key functions of the code
  • Verify that the code correctly implements the algorithm by checking if it produces expected outputs for a variety of test inputs
  • Assess the efficiency of the code by examining time complexity and space complexity.
  • Suggest specific changes or optimizations that could enhance the code’s effectiveness, citing reasons for each recommendation.

  Content

In software development, the implementation of an algorithm through programming code is not just about ensuring it works correctly but also about how effectively it performs under various conditions. An effective implementation balances correctness, efficiency, and maintainability while meeting the requirements of the task.

Equally important in this process is code optimisation, which enhances the performance of the program by refining its structure and execution. Through thoughtful optimisation, developers can create software that is faster, more resource-efficient, and scalable, all while maintaining clarity and reliability.

 

Code Effectiveness

When assessing the effective of programming code developed to implement an algorithm there are a few key points to keep in mind:

  1. Correctness: Ensure the code produces the correct output for all possible inputs. Test it with various input values, including edge cases and boundary conditions.
  2. Efficiency: Make sure the code takes the shortest possible route to solve the solution whilst not wasting resources on unnecessary or unneeded objects such as empty variables or repeated sections of code. 
  3. Readability: Assess how easily the code can be understood by other developers. Clear, well-organised code with meaningful variable names, comments, and logical structure is crucial for maintainability and collaboration.
  4. Modularity: Check if the code is broken down into modular components, each responsible for a specific task. Modular code is easier to understand, debug, and maintain.
  5. Error Handling: Evaluate how the code handles unexpected situations, such as invalid input or runtime errors. Robust error handling can prevent unexpected crashes and improve the reliability of the code.

Optimisation

Code optimisation in software engineering is the process of refining code to make it run faster, use fewer resources, and be easier to understand and maintain. This can involve things such as choosing more efficient algorithms, avoiding unnecessary calculations and organising code in a clear and logical way.

General methods of optimising code:

  • Reducing the amount of loops used within an algorithm
    • Loops are often necessary but can be costly in terms of performance, especially when they are nested or repeated unnecessarily.
    • If multiple loops iterate over the same data set, combine them into a single loop to reduce overhead.
  • Avoid unnecessary calculations
    • Perform calculations only when necessary to save processing time.
    • Calculations that do not depend on the loop index should be moved outside the loop.
    • Store results of expensive operations if they need to be used multiple times.
  • Use efficient data structures
    • Selecting the right data structure can significantly affect the performance of your code. 
    • Use sets instead of lists for checking if an item exists in a collection of items.
    • Use dictionaries for key-value pairs and fast lookups.
  • Break early from loops
    • Exiting a loop as soon as possible can save significant processing time.
    • Use conditions to break out of loops early.
  • Utilise built-in functions
    • Built-in functions are often optimised and written in lower-level languages, making them faster.
    • String Concatenation: Use ''.join() instead of + in loops.
    • Use map and filter for applying functions to collections of items.
  • Avoid deep nesting of code
    • Deeply nested code can be difficult to read, maintain, and optimise.
    • Use early returns to reduce the depth of nesting.
    • Break down deeply nested logic into separate functions.

2.8 Design and Implement OOP

Syllabus
Design and implement computer programs involving branching, iteration and functions in an OOP language for an identified need or opportunity

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Design and implement software solutions using branching, iteration, and functions within an OOP framework to address specific needs or opportunities.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Demonstrate the use of branching (if-else, switch-case statements), iteration (loops like for, while), and functions in creating software.
  • Develop a small project or a component of a larger project that utilizes OOP concepts to solve a real-world problem, documenting the process and the code effectively.

  Content

Together, branching, iteration, and functions (methods) enable developers to create more modular, reusable, and maintainable code in object-oriented systems. They help manage complexity by dividing tasks into smaller, manageable parts and defining clear interfaces for objects.

 

These are all concepts that you have learnt already, to summarise:

  • Branching involves making decisions within the program. It uses conditions to determine which blocks of code to execute. For example, if, else, and elif statements allow the program to execute different code based on different inputs or states. In OOP, branching can be used within methods to determine how an object should behave under different conditions. Refer to 1.5 Structured algorithms for more information.
  • Iteration refers to looping through data structures or repeating some action until a condition changes. Common iterators include for loops and while loops. In OOP, iteration might be used to perform actions on each item in a collection of objects, such as invoking a method on every object in a list. Refer to 1.5 Structured algorithms for more information.
  • Functions are blocks of code that perform specific tasks and can be called as needed. In OOP, these are often implemented as methods, which are functions that are associated with a specific class. Methods define behaviours for class instances and can access and modify the state of these instances. Refer to 1.8 Procedures and functions for more information.

2.9 Implement and Modify OOP

Syllabus
Implement and modify OOP programming code including:
- clear and uncluttered mainline
- one logical task per subroutine
- use of stubs
- use of control structures and data structures
- ease of maintenance
- version control
- regular backup

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand best practices in code structure, including maintaining a clear mainline, task-specific subroutines, and utilizing control and data structures effectively.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Develop a clear, uncluttered mainline and modular subroutines, each performing a single logical task, enhanced by the use of stubs for independent testing.
  • Utilise control and data structures effectively for optimal data management and decision-making.
  • Apply maintenance principles, version control, and regular backups to ensure the code is robust, easily updatable, and secure against data loss.

  Content

When writing any program we aim to create robust, maintainable and scalable software, facilitating both initial development and any future modifications. This includes:

  1. Clear and Uncluttered Mainline: The mainline logic of the program should be straightforward and free from clutter, serving as a clear entry and exit point of the application.

  2. One Logical Task per Subroutine: Each subroutine or method should handle a single logical task, enhancing readability and reusability.

  3. Use of Stubs: Stubs are temporary, simplistic implementations of methods used during the early stages of development to help test sections of the code independently by simulating the behavior of complete methods.

  4. Use of Control Structures and Data Structures: Effective use of control structures (like loops and conditionals) and data structures (like arrays, lists, and dictionaries) is crucial for managing data flow and organization within the program. 1.5 Structured algorithms

  5. Ease of Maintenance: The code should be written in a way that makes it easy to update and modify, with a clear structure and well-documented sections to assist future developers or for future reference.

  6. Version Control: Utilizing version control systems (such as Git) is essential for managing changes to the codebase, allowing multiple versions and collaborative work. 1.2 Online collaboration tools

  7. Regular Backup: Regularly backing up the code ensures safety against data loss and provides a means to revert to previous versions if necessary.

2.10 Test and Evaluate

Syllabus
Apply methodologies to test and evaluate code including:
- unit, subsystem and system testing
- black, white and grey box testing
- quality assurance

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand and apply various testing methodologies, including unit, subsystem, and system testing, along with black, white, and grey box testing, to ensure software quality and reliability.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Use OOP principles to build, document, and debug a software project that addresses a real-world problem.
  • Execute comprehensive testing strategies across different stages of the software development process and apply quality assurance practices to meet software standards.

  Content

To test and evaluate code effectively, we can apply the following methodologies:

  1. Unit, Subsystem, and System Testing:

    • Unit Testing: Tests individual components or functions of a software for correctness.
    • Subsystem Testing: Tests a complete module or subsystem for errors, typically involving multiple units.
    • System Testing: Evaluates the complete system's compliance with specified requirements.

  2. Black, White, and Grey Box Testing:

    • Black Box Testing: Testing without knowledge of the internal workings of the application, focusing on outputs in response to certain inputs and execution conditions.
    • White Box Testing: Involves testing internal structures or workings of an application, as opposed to its functionality (i.e., testing internal code logic).
    • Grey Box Testing: A combination of both black and white box testing methods where some knowledge of the internal structure is used to design test cases.

  3. Quality Assurance: Ensures that the software meets quality standards and satisfies the requirements through various practices and processes throughout the development lifecycle.

For more detailed information refer to: 1.18 Test and evaluate

3.1 Mechatronic Systems

Syllabus
Outline applications of mechatronic systems in a variety of specialised fields

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • develop an understanding of the diverse applications of mechatronic systems in various specialised fields

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • demonstrate knowledge of various applications of mechatronic systems
  • assess the role of mechatronics in modern technology

  Content
