Manufacturing and Industrial Automation

Mechatronic systems significantly enhance manufacturing processes by integrating automation, which increases precision, efficiency, and flexibility.

  • Robotic Arms: Used for tasks such as welding, painting, assembly, pick and place, and packaging. They offer high precision and can work continuously without fatigue.
  • Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs): These are used to transport materials within a factory autonomously, reducing the need for human labour and increasing operational efficiency.
  • Computer Numerical Control (CNC) Machines: These automated machining tools are controlled by a computer, allowing for the precise and complex manufacturing of parts, which is essential for maintaining high-quality production standards.

 

Automation in Vehicle Production

 

Mechatronic Industries

Automotive

In the automotive sector, mechatronic systems enhance vehicle safety, performance, and automation, leading to more reliable and intelligent vehicles.

  • Anti-lock Braking Systems (ABS): Prevents wheels from locking up during braking, which helps maintain vehicle control and reduces stopping distances, especially on slippery surfaces.
  • Electronic Stability Control (ESC): Enhances vehicle stability by detecting and reducing loss of traction, preventing skidding and rollovers.
  • Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems (ADAS): Features like adaptive cruise control, lane departure warnings, and automatic emergency braking improve driver safety and convenience by assisting with driving tasks and alerting drivers to potential hazards.

Aerospace

Mechatronic systems in aerospace contribute to enhanced control, stability, and operational efficiency of aircraft and spacecraft.

  • Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs): Also known as drones, these are used for surveillance, mapping, and delivery, providing valuable data and services with precision and flexibility.
  • Fly-by-Wire Systems: Replace traditional manual flight controls with electronic interfaces, improving aircraft performance and safety by allowing for more precise control and reducing pilot workload.
  • Satellite Attitude Control: Systems that maintain the orientation of satellites, ensuring they remain properly aligned for communication and observation tasks.

 

Aerospace Engineering

 

Medical Field

Mechatronic systems revolutionise medical technology, enhancing diagnostic, therapeutic, and surgical capabilities.

  • Surgical Robots: Provide surgeons with enhanced precision and control during minimally invasive procedures, leading to better patient outcomes and faster recovery times.
  • Prosthetics: Advanced prosthetic limbs with integrated sensors and actuators allow for more natural movement and improved functionality for amputees.
  • Diagnostic Devices: Automated systems such as blood analysers and MRI machines offer quick, accurate diagnostics, which are essential for effective treatment planning.

 

Consumer Electronics

In consumer electronics, mechatronic systems improve functionality, user experience, and connectivity.

  • Smartphones: Integrate sensors, cameras, and actuators to offer a wide range of functionalities, from high-quality photography to health monitoring.
  • Home Automation Systems: Devices like smart thermostats, lighting, and security systems enhance home comfort, energy efficiency, and security through automation and remote control.
  • Wearable Technology: Fitness trackers and smartwatches monitor health parameters, providing users with valuable data to manage their health and fitness.

 

Home Automation System Graphic

 

Agriculture

Mechatronic systems in agriculture increase efficiency, precision, and sustainability in farming practices.

  • Autonomous Tractors: Perform tasks such as ploughing, seeding, and harvesting with minimal human intervention, increasing productivity and reducing labour costs.
  • Precision Farming Equipment: Utilises GPS and sensors to optimise field management, leading to better crop yields and reduced resource usage.
  • Drones: Used for crop monitoring, spraying pesticides, and surveying large areas, providing detailed insights that help farmers make informed decisions.

 

Energy Sector

Mechatronic systems help manage and optimise energy production, distribution, and consumption.

  • Smart Grids: Integrate digital technology to manage electricity supply efficiently, improving reliability and facilitating the integration of renewable energy sources.
  • Renewable Energy Systems: Automated systems manage wind turbines and solar panels, maximising energy production and efficiency.
  • Robotic Inspection Systems: Inspect and maintain power lines and pipelines, ensuring safety and reducing downtime through early detection of issues.

 

Smart Grid Technology

 

Defence and Military

In defence and military applications, mechatronic systems enhance operational capabilities, safety, and effectiveness.

  • Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs): Used for tasks like bomb disposal and reconnaissance missions, reducing the risk to human personnel.
  • Exoskeletons: Enhance soldier capabilities by providing additional strength and endurance, improving mobility and reducing fatigue.
  • Autonomous Combat Systems: Include drones and robotic systems that can operate in combat scenarios, providing surveillance, targeting, and offensive capabilities without putting human lives at risk.

3.2 Hardware

Syllabus
Identify the hardware requirements to run a program and the effect on code development including:
assessing the relationship of microcontrollers and the central processing unit (CPU)
the influence of instruction set and opcodes
the use of address and data registers

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • develop an understanding of the hardware requirements necessary to run a program and how these requirements affect code development, including the roles and interactions of microcontrollers and CPUs, the impact of instruction sets and opcodes, and the function of address and data registers.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • assess and explain the relationship between microcontrollers and the central processing unit (CPU) in the context of code execution.
  • analyse and discuss how the instruction set and opcodes influence program functionality and performance.
  • identify and describe the roles of address and data registers in the process of program execution.
  • evaluate hardware requirements for specific programs and determine their impact on code development and performance.
  • demonstrate the ability to make informed decisions about hardware requirements based on program needs and development goals.

  Content

Different systems have different requirements. A security camera has different functions and hardware than a smart light. Depending on the requirements of each system, our microcontroller may need more pins, Bluetooth capability, or more memory. For example, a smart light would need wireless capability, whereas a security camera would need a camera attached and a powerful enough processor to look at camera data and track faces in real time. 

 

Microcontrollers

Mechatronic systems are designed to perform specific fixed tasks and, to save cost and space, they do not execute their code on a normal computer or powerful microprocessor (CPU). Mechatronic systems execute their code in a microcontroller which contains a very small microprocessor, some memory to store program code and data and input/output pins to sense and react to their environment.

To help prototype mechatronic systems, microcontrollers are widely available on circuit boards which include a method to connect and upload code. These boards are called microcontroller boards and may include extra functionality such as sensors, LEDs and buzzers.

 

Relationship of microcontrollers and the central processing unit

Most systems would include a central processing unit (CPU), which processes input and produces output. However, by itself a CPU is useless as there would be no place to store the outputs of the CPU, as well as use it to interface with the environment. In embedded systems, a microcontroller is used for this purpose. A microcontroller contains a CPU, alongside memory and registers (fast, set slots of memory stored within the CPU used for operations) to store the outputs of the CPU, as well as pins to connect peripherals to the CPU.

 


ATmega328P microcontroller. Contains the 8-bit microprocessor, registers, flash memory, and I/O lines.
From: https://www.microchip.com/en-us/product/atmega328p

 

Instruction set and opcodes

Each processor has an instruction set, which determines what instructions do based on the data that is given to the processor. The processor reads the instruction which is a number of bytes of machine code, where the bits that distinguish what instruction it is is called the opcode. The opcode tells the processor what to do, i.e. add two numbers together, move this number into memory. We can use the CHIP-8 programming language as an example as it uses opcodes as lines of code.

Note that CHIP-8 is not an instruction but is solely a teaching example in these notes

An opcode in CHIP-8 takes the form of ZZZZ where Z is a hexadecimal number. The opcode for adding two numbers is 8XY4, where X and Y specify the register slot. If we wanted to add two numbers together and the numbers were in registers 1 and 2, our instruction would be 8124.

Example excerpt from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHIP-8

We can differentiate between types of CPU instruction sets, which are complex instruction set computers (CISC) and reduced instruction set computers (RISC). CISCs are processors in which opcodes can specify the processor to perform multiple low-level instructions in one opcode, including high-level abstracted instructions such as control flow. RISCs are processors which have two separate types of instructions, which are instructions that load and store from memory and registers, and instructions that use the ALU in conjunction with registers. This means to add a number, it cannot be in memory, it must be in the CPU registers. Thus CISC uses less instructions and system resources but is slower and more power hungry, while RISC uses more instructions and system resources but is faster and more efficient.

 

RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computers)

Advantages

Disadvantages
  • Less power draw
  • Simpler
  • Faster execution speed
  • More instructions needed
  • Larger executable size
  • More memory required

 

CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computers)

Advantages

Disadvantages
  • Less instructions needed
  • Smaller executable size
  • Less memory required
  • More power draw
  • Complex
  • Slower execution speed

 

For example, the RISC instruction set, ARM, has instructions which are generally 4 bytes in length, while x86 - which is regarded as a CISC instruction set - has instructions that may be anywhere from 1 byte to 15 bytes in length.

Please note that current instructions sets may include features of both CISC and RISC

 

The use of address and data registers

To identify the hardware requirements to run a program and the effect on code development, we must understand the role and use of address and data registers in computing systems.

 

Hardware Requirements and Address Registers

Different programs require different hardware capabilities, depending on their complexity and purpose. Address and data registers are critical components of a computer's central processing unit (CPU) and play a vital role in program execution.

Address Registers: These are special-purpose registers used to store memory addresses. They are essential for accessing and managing memory locations during program execution. For instance, a program that performs extensive data manipulation might require a CPU with multiple address registers to handle the addresses of various data points efficiently. Address registers facilitate the CPU in quickly accessing specific memory locations, which is crucial for both reading from and writing to memory.

 

Data Registers and Their Impact on Code Development

Data Registers: These are used to store actual data values that the CPU needs to process. The number and size of data registers directly impact a program's performance and the complexity of operations it can perform. For example, a program that involves heavy numerical computations would benefit from having a CPU with larger and more numerous data registers, allowing it to handle more data simultaneously and execute complex instructions more efficiently.

 

Example of Use in Code Development

To illustrate, consider a simple arithmetic operation in assembly language:

MOV R1, #5     ; Move the value 5 into register R1
MOV R2, #10    ; Move the value 10 into register R2
ADD R3, R1, R2 ; Add the values in R1 and R2, store the result in R3

In this example:
- `R1`, `R2`, and `R3` are data registers.
- The CPU uses address registers internally to fetch the instructions and operands from memory.
- The `MOV` instructions place data into the data registers.
- The `ADD` instruction performs the operation using the data in these registers.

 

Effect on Code Development

The availability and design of address and data registers influence how programmers write and optimise their code. For instance, a CPU with a limited number of registers might require more frequent access to slower main memory, leading to potential performance bottlenecks. Conversely, a CPU with ample registers can perform more operations in parallel and reduce the need for memory accesses, leading to more efficient and faster code execution.

In summary, the hardware requirements to run a program, particularly the use of address and data registers, significantly affect how code is developed and optimised. Understanding these requirements helps in choosing the right hardware for specific applications and in writing efficient, high-performance programs.

3.3 Sensors/Actuators

Syllabus
Identify and describe a range of sensors, actuators and end effectors/manipulators within existing mechatronic systems including:
motion sensors
light level sensors
hydraulic actuators
robotic grippers

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • be able to identify and describe the functions and applications of various sensors, actuators, and end effectors/manipulators in existing mechatronic systems.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • identify and describe the purpose and operation of motion sensors, light level sensors, hydraulic actuators, and robotic grippers.
  • outline examples of mechatronic systems that use these components and explain their roles within the system.  
  • analyse the advantages and limitations of using these sensors, actuators, and end effectors/manipulators in different mechatronic applications.
  • discuss how these components enhance the performance and functionality of mechatronic systems, using specific case studies or examples.

  Content

 

▶ Video won't play offline. Watch on Canvas · all modules
https://view.genially.com/66736fd3f2c1f0001490a1ea

 

Inputs – transducers and sensors

An electronic transducer is a small device that converts energy from one form into electricity.

The conversion uses no separate signal processing, and the resultant output signal is often too small for many microcontrollers to use directly.

Different transducers can convert sound, pressure, temperature, capacitance, torque and other environmental factors to electricity.

A sensor is a device that uses an appropriate transducer to measure an environmental quantity and convert it into an electrical signal appropriate for use in common microcontrollers.

Sensors are generally connected directly to a microcontroller or microcontroller board which can be programmed to read in the sensor value and process it with logic to determine the next appropriate actions.

 

Outputs – actuators and end effectors

Actuators and end effectors provide the outputs for movement of mechatronic systems.

Actuators are motors that produce rotational or linear movement and, in some cases, may be all that is required for parts of a system.

When more complex movement is desired, end effectors are used to convert the basic movement of an actuator, or a collection of actuators, to create more complex movement.

Examples of end effectors include a robotic gripper and movement in a mechatronic prosthesis.

 

Examples of Sensors and Actuators

 

Motion Sensors

Motion sensors detect and measure various forms of movement, changes in position, and orientation. These are essential for providing feedback and control in dynamic systems.

  • Accelerometers: Measure the rate of change of velocity to detect acceleration.
    • Applications: Used in smartphones for screen orientation, drones for stabilisation, and automotive systems for crash detection.
  • Gyroscopes: Measure the rate of rotation around an axis to track angular movement.
    • Applications: Utilised in navigation systems for orientation, stabilisation of cameras, and balance control in robots.
  • Infrared (IR) Sensors: Detect motion by measuring changes in infrared light emitted by objects.
    • Applications: Common in security systems for motion detection, automatic doors for activation, and in robotics for obstacle detection.
  • Ultrasonic Sensors: Use sound waves to measure the distance to an object by timing the echo return.
    • Applications: Widely used in autonomous vehicles for distance measurement and collision avoidance, as well as in industrial automation for object detection.

Light Level Sensor

Light level sensors measure the intensity of light in an environment, crucial for applications requiring light sensitivity and control.

  • Photodiodes: Convert light into an electrical current proportional to the light intensity.
    • Applications: Employed in light meters for precise measurement, camera systems for exposure control, and automatic lighting systems for environmental adaptation.
  • Photoresistors (LDRs): Change resistance based on the intensity of incident light.
    • Applications: Used in street lighting systems that turn on/off automatically, alarm devices that respond to light changes, and solar garden lights.
  • Light-to-Frequency Converters: Convert light intensity to a corresponding frequency signal.
    • Applications: Applied in colour sensing for quality control, ambient light sensing in electronic devices, and optical communication systems.

Hydraulic Actuators

Hydraulic actuators convert hydraulic energy into mechanical motion, vital for applications requiring high force and precise control.

  • Linear Hydraulic Actuators: Use hydraulic fluid to create linear motion.
    • Applications: Utilised in construction equipment for lifting and moving heavy loads, industrial machinery for precise positioning, and aircraft landing gear systems for reliable deployment and retraction.
  • Rotary Hydraulic Actuators: Use hydraulic fluid to produce rotational motion.
    • Applications: Employed in conveyor systems for rotation control, robotics for joint actuation, and marine steering systems for precise directional control.
  • Hydraulic Cylinders: Convert fluid power into linear mechanical force and motion.
    • Applications: Used in hydraulic presses for shaping materials, automotive systems for braking and suspension, and agricultural machinery for lifting and tilting mechanisms.

Robotic Grippers

Robotic grippers are devices attached to the end of a robotic arm, essential for manipulating objects in various applications.

  • Parallel Grippers: Use two fingers that move parallel to each other to grasp objects.
    • Applications: Utilised in manufacturing for assembly and packaging, electronics for handling delicate components, and laboratories for precise sample manipulation.
  • Vacuum Grippers: Use suction cups to hold objects by creating a vacuum.
    • Applications: Employed in material handling for picking and placing flat objects, logistics for palletising and depalletising boxes, and food processing for handling irregularly shaped items.
  • Magnetic Grippers: Use magnetic force to attract and hold ferromagnetic materials.
    • Applications: Used in metalworking for handling sheet metals, recycling for sorting magnetic materials, and automotive assembly for manipulating metal parts.

 

   Key Terminology

  • End Effector - End effectors are specific types of actuators attached to the end of a robotic arm that interact directly with the environment (e.g., grippers, welding torches). While all end effectors are actuators, not all actuators are end effectors.
  • Manipulators - Manipulators use both sensors and actuators to perform tasks. Sensors provide the necessary information about the environment (e.g., object location), actuators perform the required movements, and the manipulator integrates these components to achieve the desired task.

3.4 Data

Syllabus
Use different types of data and understand how it is obtained and processed in a mechatronic system, including diagnostic data and data used for optimisation

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • develop an understanding of different types of data and how it is obtained and processed in a mechatronic system, including diagnostic data and data used for optimisation

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • identify various types of data used in mechatronic systems
  • explain how data is obtained in mechatronic systems
  • describe the processes for handling and processing data in mechatronic systems
  • analyse the role of diagnostic data in system performance
  • evaluate the importance of data optimisation in mechatronic systems

  Content

When building mechatronic systems, data is gathered within the system and from the environment to regulate the system and maintain it, so as to make sure the system achieves its purpose in an efficient manner.

 

Sensor Data

Types of Sensors

Data in mechatronic systems are given from sensors connected to the microcontroller. Sensors can either be analog or digital, where analog sensors give a range of values whereas digital sensors give a boolean value (HIGH or LOW, which is the value of VCC and GND). Analog sensors include potentiometers (dials), temperature sensors, pressure sensors, light sensors. Digital sensors include digital buttons such as light switches, keyboard switches, or sensors such as knock sensors.

Arduino pin diagram. VCC refers to control power which will be +5V or +3V3.
From: https://docs.arduino.cc/retired/boards/arduino-uno-rev3-with-long-pins/

Sensor Construction

Analog sensors are typically connected with at least three wires, one to ground pin, one to power, and one to data. To get a reading from the sensor, the sensor sends a current at a specific voltage to the data pin, allowing the microcontroller to convert the voltage reading to a value. The ground and power pins are used as LOW and HIGH references respectively as a reference for the voltage reading given by the sensor.

Digital sensors such as buttons typically include only two pins which are typically connected to GND and data pins. When pressing the button with solely those wires, the voltage reading at the data pin is floating, meaning it is undefined. To get a solid reading there needs to be a pullup or pulldown resistor connected to the wire, which is connected to VCC.

From: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potentiometer#/media/File:Electronic-Component-Potentiometer.jpg

ADC

In the case of an analog sensor, the voltage signal needs to be converted into a digital value by an analog to digital converter (ADC), as digital computers can only manipulate discrete data and not the analog continuous voltage signal. The ADC samples the analog input at normal intervals to build a discrete snapshot of the continuous data, which converts the continuous signal into a digital bit format at each time interval. This would be similar to a histogram.

From: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog-to-digital_converter#/media/File:Conversion_AD_DA.png

With digital sensors, they will only give HIGH or LOW voltage readings, which is the value of power and ground respectively, and this will be read by the microcontroller pin which will read the signal as LOW unless it passes a set voltage threshold to be HIGH. The reason is that sometimes the signal will have voltage drops so the sensor will need to account for this.

 

 

Protocol Bus (I2C)

Oftentimes we may want to use multiple peripherals despite only having a limited number of pins. To use multiple peripherals while only using two wires, the I2C protocol bus can be used. I2C functions by having the master controller - typically the microcontroller - request for a read or write from a specific peripheral based on its address, then having data sent across the bus. Data is sent across the bus through the SDA (Serial Data) pin bit by bit, which is synced by a clock signal sent by the master device on SCL (Serial Clock). This means that a bit is sent whenever the clock signal is at HIGH or LOW.

An I2C message starts with the master sending the 7 bit address of the peripheral across the bus which tells it which peripheral to be read or written to. Then it sends 1 bit to signify a read or write operation. The peripheral then sends an acknowledgement bit to acknowledge that the information has been received. Then data is sent in 8 bits from either the controller or peripheral, and then the receiver sends an acknowledgement bit to receive the next chunk of data.

From: https://docs.arduino.cc/learn/communication/wire/

 

 

Controlling actuators and PWM signals

Data is used to control actuators such as DC motors. Since microcontrollers control signals and motors require large amounts of current, motor drivers with external power sources not from the microcontroller are used to power motors.

For actuators with digital input, they are typically controlled by sending a pulse width modulated (PWM) signal. A PWM signal is a digital signal that sends data by encoding the data as the period of HIGH pulses within the signal. The percentage of time the signal is on is called the duty cycle, so a signal that is always on has a duty cycle of 100% which would be full power, and a signal that is always off has a duty cycle of 0% which would be grounded. To control an LED to be at half power, the microcontroller can send a PWM signal at a duty cycle of 50%. For the LED, the frequency of the signal should be fast enough to be invisible to the eye.

From: https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/pulse-width-modulation/all

Mechatronic systems also typically use servo motors. Servo motors, unlike DC motors, do not have speed, but instead have position as they rotate their axle from one specific angle to another specific angle. Most servo motors expect an update every 20ms with a pulse between 1 to 2ms, i.e. a 5% to 10% duty cycle. At a 5% duty cycle the servo motor will be at 0 degrees and at 10% it will be at 180 degrees, thus a pulse at 1.5ms will rotate the motor to be at 90 degrees. Therefore to rotate the servo motor at a specific position in between, the microcontroller must send a signal between 1 and 2ms.

 

Feedback Loop

Mechatronic systems are typically driven in a continuous feedback loop that takes in environmental data gathered by sensors to ensure optimal usage of actuators. A commonly used controller for these systems is PID (proportional, integral, derivative). For example, a line follow wheeled robot is tasked with following a black line on the floor, so its sensor picks up the deviation from the line which then tells the motors how to move. Once the robot moves, this then affects the readings taken by the sensor. Therefore the system must optimise by moving the motors in a path that reduces the deviance from the line. To minimise deviance, we can use the PID controller which attempts to minimise deviance from a target by moving the actuators in accordance to three terms.

 

1. Proportional: Term that corrects for current error

2. Integral: Term that corrects for past error

3. Derivative: Term that corrects for the error's rate of change

 

In real world applications, PID is used to automatically correct errors, sometimes this will be error along a path, such as in car cruise controls, or controlled variables such as temperature by setting a target temperature.

Diagram of typical PID system. System corrects for the initial error, which causes an overshoot which is correcting, creating an oscillating pattern until it settles on the target.
From: https://www.ni.com/en/shop/labview/pid-theory-explained.html

Cycle 12 (Term 3: Weeks 3-4) Mechatronics

3.5 Software

Syllabus
Experiment with software to control interactions and dependencies within mechatronic systems including:
motion constraints
degrees of freedom
combination of subsystems
combination of sensors, actuators and end effectors to create viable subsystems

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • be able to experiment with software to control interactions and dependencies within mechatronic systems.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • demonstrate the ability to control motion constraints and understand their importance in mechatronic systems.
  • explain and manipulate the degrees of freedom in various components of mechatronic systems.
  • combine different subsystems effectively to achieve desired outcomes in mechatronic projects.
  • integrate sensors, actuators, and end effectors to create and control viable subsystems, providing examples of their applications.
  • evaluate the performance of their mechatronic systems through experimentation and provide insights on improvements and optimisations.

  Content

Mechatronic systems combine mechanical, electrical, and software components to perform complex, automated tasks. To design and control these systems effectively, software tools play a critical role in managing the interactions and dependencies between components.

 

Motion Constraints

Motion constraints refer to the limits placed on the movement of mechanical components within the system. Software can manage these constraints by:

  1. Kinematic Analysis and Planning: Algorithms calculate the permissible range of movements for each joint or actuator to prevent collisions or exceeding design limits.
  2. Real-time Monitoring and Feedback: Sensors provide real-time data on the position, speed, and acceleration of moving parts. The software processes this data to ensure the components stay within the predefined motion constraints.
  3. Error Correction: If the system detects a deviation from the allowed motion, the software can make real-time adjustments to correct the trajectory or halt the system to prevent damage.

Degrees of Freedom

Degrees of freedom (DOF) describe the number of independent movements a system can perform. Software manages DOF by:

  1. Control Algorithms: Implementing control algorithms like PID (Proportional-Integral-Derivative) to manage the movement in each degree of freedom precisely.
  2. Inverse Kinematics: Calculating the necessary joint movements to achieve a desired position and orientation of the end effector.
  3. Path Planning: Developing trajectories that the system should follow, considering all degrees of freedom to achieve smooth and efficient movements.

Combination Subsystems

Combining various subsystems into a coherent mechatronic system involves:

  1. Integration Middleware: Software that provides a common platform for communication between different subsystems, ensuring they work together seamlessly.
  2. Hierarchical Control Systems: Structuring control systems in a hierarchy where high-level software manages overall system behaviour while lower-level software handles specific subsystems.
  3. Simulation and Testing: Using software tools to simulate the integrated subsystems, allowing for testing and validation before actual deployment.

Combination of Components

Creating viable subsystems with sensors, actuators, and end effectors involves:

  1. Sensor Fusion: Integrating data from multiple sensors to provide a comprehensive understanding of the system’s state and environment.
  2. Actuator Control: Software algorithms translate high-level commands into precise actions by the actuators, ensuring accurate movement and force application.
  3. Coordination: Synchronising the actions of sensors, actuators, and end effectors to perform complex tasks. This involves real-time data processing and control logic to ensure cohesive operation.
  4. Feedback Loops: Establishing closed-loop control systems where sensors provide feedback to adjust the actions of actuators in real-time, maintaining desired performance and compensating for disturbances.

 

Example Scenario: Robotic Arm

Consider a robotic arm with multiple joints (degrees of freedom), equipped with sensors for position and force, and end effectors for handling objects:

  1. Motion Constraints: Software ensures the arm doesn’t extend beyond its physical limits or collide with other objects.
  2. Degrees of Freedom: Control algorithms manage the arm’s joints to move in 3D space, ensuring smooth and accurate positioning.
  3. Combination of Subsystems: The arm’s base, joints, and gripper work together, coordinated by software that integrates motion control, sensor data, and end effector commands.
  4. Combination of Sensors, Actuators, and End Effectors: Sensors provide feedback on the arm’s position and the force applied by the gripper. The software processes this data to adjust the actuators, ensuring the gripper picks up and moves objects as intended.

3.6 Mechatronic Components

Syllabus
Determine power, battery and material requirements for components of a mechatronic system

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • be able to determine the power, battery, and material requirements for components of a mechatronic system.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • calculate the power requirements for various components within a mechatronic system.
  • assess and select appropriate battery types and capacities to meet the power needs of the system.
  • identify suitable materials for different components, considering factors like durability, weight, and cost.
  • provide examples of how power, battery, and material choices impact the performance and efficiency of a mechatronic system.
  • justify their choices of power sources, battery types, and materials based on the specific requirements and constraints of the mechatronic project.

  Content

In mechatronic systems, ensuring that each component functions efficiently and reliably requires careful consideration of its power, battery, and material requirements. These systems combine mechanical, electrical, and control elements, each with unique energy demands and operational stresses.

To achieve optimal performance, it is essential to:

  • Determine power requirements for motors, sensors, controllers, and other components.
  • Calculate battery specifications to meet energy needs and ensure uninterrupted operation.
  • Select appropriate materials that provide strength, durability, and thermal or electrical efficiency.

 

Microcontroller/Processor

The microcontroller or processor is the brain of the mechatronic system. It performs all the computations and controls the other components.

    •    Power Consumption: Typically ranges from 0.5 mW to 500 mW, depending on complexity and processing power.
    •    Voltage: Common operating voltages are 3.3V or 5V.
    •    Current: Ranges from a few microamps in sleep mode to tens of milliamps during operation.
    •    Power Management: Sleep modes and power-efficient coding can reduce power consumption.

Sensors

Sensors detect various physical parameters such as temperature, pressure, light, and motion.

    •    Power Consumption: Varies widely, from a few microwatts to several watts.
    •    Voltage: Typically between 1.8V and 5V.
    •    Current: Ranges from microamps to hundreds of milliamps.
    •    Types: Simple sensors like temperature sensors consume less power compared to complex ones like LiDAR.

Actuators

Actuators are responsible for moving or controlling a mechanism or system.

    •    Power Consumption: Can range from a few watts to several hundred watts.
    •    Voltage: Commonly 6V, 12V, or 24V.
    •    Current: Can range from hundreds of milliamps to several amps.
    •    Types: DC motors, stepper motors, and servo motors have varying power needs based on their load and application.

Communication Modules

Communication modules enable the mechatronic system to interact with other devices or networks.

    •    Power Consumption: Typically between 50 mW to 1W.
    •    Voltage: Common operating voltages are 3.3V or 5V.
    •    Current: Ranges from a few milliamps to several hundred milliamps.
    •    Types: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and Zigbee modules have different power profiles.

3.7 Wiring Diagrams

Syllabus
Develop wiring diagrams for a mechatronic system, considering data and power supply requirements

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • develop wiring diagrams for a mechatronic system, considering data and power supply requirements

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • identify the components required for wiring a mechatronic system
  • explain the data and power supply requirements for the system
  • design wiring diagrams that integrate both data and power supply elements
  • demonstrate the correct connections for data and power supply in a wiring diagram

  Content

From Course Specifications

“If a wiring diagram requires other electrical components, the components must be clearly labelled for identification”

 

Usage of electrical components

Capacitors

Capacitors

  • Used to store energy
  • Decouples components and bypasses power supply voltage drops
    • Removes voltage ripples and suppresses high frequency noise in power supply
    • If voltage drops, capacitor can supply power at correct voltage
  • Filters diode rectified AC signals into a DC-like signal
  • Filters signals of specific frequencies

 

  • How data relates to each other and moves through a system
  • How energy is managed in a system

Diodes

Diodes

  • Acts as a one-way switch for current
  • Rectifies AC signals (removes negative signal) to turn into DC with capacitors
  • Protects reverse current
  • Suppress voltage spikes

Resistors

Resistors

  • Adds resistance to a circuit
  • Limits current for components that need small current and increases voltage for components that need more voltage
  • Used as a pull-up resistor which biases pins to either HIGH or LOW
    • Also prevents shorts with circuits that connect GND to VCC

 

From: https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/pull-up-resistors

 

To wire a microcontroller, the GND pin of each component should be connected to a common ground point, which is typically the microcontroller’s GND pin. For most sensors, to drive the component the VCC pin of the microcontroller would be enough to power, however for motor drivers they would usually require more voltage, therefore depending on the component we may instead wire a separate power supply to the component. Keep in mind the ground must be common, therefore the supply’s ground is also wired to the microcontroller by having a single point where the ground of the separate power supply is wired to the ground of the microcontroller.

3.8 Design and Function

Syllabus
Determine specialist requirements that influence the design and functions of mechatronic systems designed for people with disability

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • develop an understanding of specialist requirements that influence the design and functions of mechatronic systems designed for people with disability

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • identify specialist requirements for people with disability
  • explain how these requirements impact the design of mechatronic systems
  • analyse the functions of mechatronic systems tailored for people with disability
  • evaluate the effectiveness of mechatronic systems in meeting the needs of people with disability
  • demonstrate an understanding of inclusive design principles in mechatronic systems

  Content

Mechatronic systems are used to support people, including enhancing the quality of life of those with disability. Often this will mean requirements will be made from problems that the system aims to solve or mitigate which are caused by the disability. For example, for users who are wheelchair bound, they would require a way to move around without assistance therefore their wheelchair would need a way to take in input from their users hands, be it with a touchscreen, a steering wheel, or lever, and have that drive the movement in the wheels of the wheelchair which would need to be attached to motors to drive movement.

Mechatronic systems designed for people without disability should also have considerations for those with disability to allow as many people to utilise it. A common case would be designing textual information with not only text, but also braille and also aural communication.

3.10 Open & Closed Control Systems

Syllabus
Explore the algorithmic patterns, code and applications for open and closed control systems

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • understand the fundamental concepts and differences between open and closed control systems.
  • explore algorithmic patterns and coding practices used in the development of these systems.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • identify and describe examples of open and closed control systems in various applications.
  • develop basic algorithms that simulate the behavior of open and closed control systems.
  • analyse and compare the efficiency and applications of these systems in real-world scenarios.

  Content

 

Definitions and Basic Concepts

Open Control Systems (Open Loop Systems): Open control systems operate without feedback. Rather, these perform their functions based solely on input data and a pre-set sequence of operations

Closed Control Systems (Closed Loop Systems): Closed control systems used feedback to control their operations. They continuously monitor the output and adjust it by comparing it to a desired set point via a feedback loop. This process helps in maintaining the desired level of performance despite external disturbances

 

Algorithmic Patterns

Open Loop Systems:

The algorithm in an open loop system generally will follow a straightforward sequence:

  1. Receive data input
  2. Process the input based on pre-defined settings or configurations
  3. Output the result directly without and feedback consideration

 

Here is an example of an algorithm an open loop system may follow in Python:

Notice how the algorithm never gets an feedback, the movements it performs are all pre-defined and hardcoded into it.

 

Closed Loop Systems:

Closed loop systems incorporate feedback to adjust their behaviour dynamically:

  1. Set the goal, decide what you want the output to be
  2. Continuously measure the actual output of the system
  3. Check the difference between the desired output and the actual output
  4. Use the difference to make adjustments. If the actual output is too low, increase it; if its too high, decrease it
  5. Repeat until the desired goal is met

 

Take a look at this example of a closed control system:

The algorithm continues to loop until the robot reaches the margin of the target distance, using the feedback from the position to calculate the correct position.

 

Applications

Examples of Open Loop Systems may include:

  • Simple household appliances like toasters and microwave ovens,
  • Washing machines,
  • Heating elements where precision is not critical.

Examples of Closed Loop Systems may include:

  • Automotive systems like cruise control and advanced breaking systems,
  • Industrial automation systems, including robotics and assembly lines,
  • Aerospace applications like autopilot and altitude control,
  • Home heating and air conditioning systems for maintaining temperature.

3.11 Autonomous Control

Syllabus
Outline the features of an algorithm and program code used for autonomous control

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • understand the key features of an algorithm and program code used for autonomous control.
  • be able to identify and outline the components that make up an algorithm and program code for autonomous system

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • explain the main features of an algorithm used in autonomous control systems, including input, output, processing, and decision-making steps.
  • describe the structure and elements of program code necessary for autonomous control, such as loops, conditionals, and functions.
  • develop a basic algorithm and corresponding program code that demonstrates autonomous control in a given scenario.
  • test and debug the program code to ensure it performs the intended autonomous functions accurately.
  • evaluate the effectiveness of their algorithm and program code in achieving autonomous control and suggest potential improvements for optimization and efficiency.

  Content

Autonomous control refers to the capability of a system to operate independently, making decisions and performing tasks without human intervention. This involves using sensors, algorithms, and actuators to perceive the environment, plan actions, and execute commands. Autonomous control systems are widely used in various applications, such as self-driving cars, drones, robotics, and industrial automation.

 

Autonomous control algorithms manage mechatronic systems by sensing the system state, calculating the error from a desired setpoint, and computing the required control values. This process repeats continuously in a control loop. The three common types of algorithms are:

On/Off Control (Bang-Bang Control)

Functionality:

  • Turns actuators fully on or fully off based on the system state relative to the desired setpoint.
  • Operates in a binary manner, switching between two extremes.

Strengths:

  • Simple to implement.
  • Suitable for systems where precise control is unnecessary.

Weaknesses:

  • Tends to overshoot or undershoot the setpoint.
  • Can cause oscillations as the system repeatedly hits its limits.

Additional Feature: Hysteresis:

To reduce rapid switching and potential damage to components, a tolerance band around the setpoint is introduced. This creates stability by ensuring the system only activates when deviations exceed a certain threshold.

Proportional Control

Functionality:

  • Adjusts the actuator’s response proportionally to the error (the difference between the system state and the desired setpoint).
  • The larger the error, the stronger the response.

Strengths:

  • Smoother and more refined control compared to on/off systems.
  • Reduces oscillations by varying the strength of the response.

Weaknesses:

  • When the error is small, the control signal may be too weak to move actuators effectively.
  • Can result in steady-state errors, where the system stabilises near, but not exactly at, the setpoint.

PID Control (Proportional-Integral-Derivative)

PID control enhances proportional control by adding two components: integral and derivative control.

Proportional Component (P):

  • Provides immediate adjustments based on the size of the error.

Integral Component (I):

  • Accumulates past errors over time.
  • Helps eliminate steady-state errors by ensuring that small deviations are corrected gradually.

Derivative Component (D):

  • Reacts to the rate of change in error.
  • Dampens overshoot by reducing the control response as the system approaches the setpoint too quickly.

Strengths:

  • Combines the benefits of proportional, integral, and derivative control for precise and stable operation.
  • Adapts to dynamic conditions, correcting both short-term and long-term deviations.

Weaknesses:

  • More complex to configure due to the need to tune proportional, integral, and derivative gains.
  • Can be computationally intensive for some systems.

 

 

Features of an Algorithm for Autonomous Control

 

Sensor Integration

Usage in Autonomous Control: Sensors provide real-time data about the environment. This data is crucial for making informed decisions and executing precise actions.

    •    Data Acquisition: Collecting data from various sensors like GPS, LIDAR and cameras.
    •    Sensor Fusion: Combining data from multiple sensors to create a comprehensive understanding of the environment.

Perception

Usage in Autonomous Control: Perception allows the system to interpret and understand its surroundings, which is essential for safe and efficient operation.

    •    Object Detection and Classification: Identifying and classifying objects in the environment.
    •    Environment Mapping: Creating and updating a map of the surroundings.
    •    Localisation: Determining the system’s position within the map.

Decision Making

Usage in Autonomous Control: Decision-making algorithms determine the best course of action based on the current situation and goals.

    •    Path Planning: Generating an optimal path to the destination, considering obstacles and objectives.
    •    Behaviour Planning: Deciding on high-level actions based on the current situation (e.g., lane changing, stopping).

Control

Usage in Autonomous Control: Control algorithms convert decisions into actionable commands to guide the system’s movement and actions.

    •    Motion Control: Converting path planning into executable commands for actuators (e.g., steering, acceleration, braking).
    •    Trajectory Tracking: Ensuring the system follows the planned path accurately.

Communication

Usage in Autonomous Control: Communication ensures coordination within the system and with external entities, enhancing situational awareness and safety.

    •    Inter-System Communication: Exchanging data between different parts of the system (e.g., sensors, controllers).
    •    External Communication: Interfacing with external systems (e.g., traffic signals, other vehicles).

Safety and Redundancy

Usage in Autonomous Control: Safety mechanisms and redundancy are critical to handle errors and ensure continuous operation in case of failures.

    •    Error Handling: Detecting and responding to errors or failures in the system.
    •    Fail-Safe Mechanisms: Implementing backup systems to maintain control if the primary system fails.

 

Features of Program Code for Autonomous Control

Let's consider how all of these different features come together by thinking about Autonomous Control in VexVR.

 

  1. Sensor Integration


        •    Purpose: This step collects data from multiple sensors. In this example, we use the distance sensor to measure the distance to objects and the gyro sensor to measure the robot’s orientation.
        •    Relevance to Autonomous Control: Gathering accurate and real-time data from sensors is crucial for the robot to understand its environment and make informed decisions.

  2. Perception


        •    Purpose: This step involves interpreting sensor data to detect objects and determine the robot’s position.
        •    Relevance to Autonomous Control: Perception allows the robot to recognize obstacles and know its orientation, which is essential for navigating and performing tasks safely and effectively.

  3. Decision Making


        •    Purpose: This step involves deciding the actions the robot should take based on its perception of the environment.
        •    Relevance to Autonomous Control: Effective decision-making is crucial for the robot to navigate towards its goal while avoiding obstacles. The path planning function creates a sequence of movements, and behavior planning determines whether to proceed or stop based on detected objects.

  4. Control

        •    Purpose: This step converts the planned actions into executable commands for the robot.
        •    Relevance to Autonomous Control: Control algorithms ensure that the robot moves as intended, following the planned path and adjusting its actions based on real-time feedback.

  5. Communication


        •    Purpose: This step involves sharing information within the system and with external entities.
        •    Relevance to Autonomous Control: Effective communication helps in monitoring the system’s state and coordinating actions, which is essential for maintaining situational awareness and safety.

  6. Safety and Redundancy

  7. Putting It All Together

        •    Purpose: The main control loop orchestrates all the steps, ensuring the robot continuously gathers sensor data, perceives the environment, makes decisions, controls movements, communicates data, and handles errors.
        •    Relevance to Autonomous Control: The control loop integrates all components of the autonomous system, allowing the robot to operate independently and adapt to changing conditions in real-time.

3.12 Design/Develop

Syllabus
Design, develop and produce a mechatronic system for a real-world problem including:
software control
mechanical engineering
electronics and mathematics

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Students will understand how to design, develop, and produce a mechatronic system for a real-world problem, integrating software control, mechanical engineering, electronics, and mathematics.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Students can design a mechatronic system, develop and implement software control, apply mechanical engineering principles, integrate electronics, and utilize mathematics to solve real-world problems.

  Content

 

Software Control

Software Control involves using computer programs to manage, operate and monitor mechanical and electronic system. This includes algorithms, user interfaces and real-time processing that ensure the system operates correctly and efficiently.

Role in Mechatronic Systems:

  • Control Algorithms: Software control implements algorithms that dictate how the system responds to different inputs and conditions. For example, in a robotic arms, software determines the precise movements required to pick up an object.
  • Data Processing: Software processes data from sensors to make real-time decisions. For example, an autonomous vehicle uses software to process data from cameras and LIDAR to navigate safely
  • User Interface: Software provides interfaces for users to interact with the system, such as touch screens or remote controls

 

Applications:

  • Robotics
  • Automation Systems
  • Automotive Systems

Mechanical Engineering

Mechanical Engineering involves using principles of physics, mathematics, and materials science to design, analyse, manufacture, and maintain mechanical systems. This includes the application of these principles to ensure the systems operate efficiently and effectively.

 

Role in Mechatronic Systems:

  • Structural Design: Mechanical engineering provides the structural design and analysis required for mechatronic systems. For example, in a robotic arm, mechanical engineering determines the materials and structural configuration to ensure strength and durability.
  • Dynamics and Kinematics: Mechanical engineers analyze and design the motion of mechanical systems. For instance, they determine the movement and forces in mechanisms, ensuring precise and efficient operation.
  • Thermal Management: Mechanical engineering involves managing the thermal aspects of mechatronic systems. For example, in electronic devices, mechanical engineers design cooling systems to prevent overheating.

 

Applications:

  • Robotics
  • Automotive Systems
  • Aerospace Systems

Electronics

Electronics involves using electrical circuits and components to design and develop devices that manage electrical energy and signals. This includes the development of integrated circuits, microcontrollers, and power electronics that are critical for system functionality.

 

Role in Mechatronic Systems:

  • Circuit Design: Electronics involves designing circuits that control and power mechanical systems. For example, in an autonomous vehicle, electronic circuits manage sensor inputs and motor outputs.
  • Signal Processing: Electronic systems process signals from sensors to make real-time decisions. For instance, electronic circuits in a drone process signals to stabilise and control flight.
  • Power Management: Electronics ensures efficient power management within the system. For example, in a wearable device, electronic circuits manage battery power to extend operational life.

 

Applications:

  • Consumer Electronics
  • Medical Devices
  • Industrial Automation

Mathematics

Mathematics involves using mathematical theories and techniques to model, analyse, and solve problems in various fields. This includes the application of mathematics to ensure accuracy and optimisation in system design and operation.

 

Role in Mechatronic Systems:

  • Modeling and Simulation: Mathematics is used to model and simulate the behaviour of mechatronic systems. For example, mathematical models predict the performance of a robotic system under different conditions.
  • Optimisation: Mathematics is used to optimise the design and operation of systems. For instance, algorithms optimise the path planning for autonomous robots to minimise energy consumption.
  • Control Theory: Mathematical principles underpin control theory, which governs how systems respond to inputs. For example, control algorithms use mathematics to ensure stability and performance in automated systems.

 

Applications:

  • Robotics
  • Telecommunications
  • Engineering Design

 

Applications: VexCode VR

3.13 Implement

Syllabus
Implement algorithms and design programming code to drive mechatronic devices

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • learn to implement algorithms and design programming code to control and drive mechatronic devices, integrating both software and hardware components to achieve specified tasks.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • create and implement algorithms to effectively control mechatronic devices.
  • design and write programming code that integrates with mechatronic hardware, ensuring proper functionality and performance.

  Content

 

Implementation: VexCode VR

Open up VexCode VR, create and next text project and select the playground Hidden Pixel Art.

 

Let's have a go at applying what you have learnt about algorithms in this exercise.

 

Discover the Hidden Pixel Art by navigating around the entire Playground surface under the gold colored roof. Each pixel in the Hidden Pixel Art is 1 grid square in size, and the entire Hidden Pixel Art is 8 pixels by 8 pixels in size. Filled pixels will report to the Down Eye Sensor as ‘Green’ and empty pixels will report to the Down Eye Sensor as ‘Blue.’

 

Level 1: Using a piece of paper, create an 8 x 8 grid. Program the VR Robot to navigate across the Hidden Pixel Art Playground. While the VR Robot is driving, use the Dashboard to observe and record the color value of the Down Eye Sensor on the paper 8 x 8 grid. The colors recorded on your 8 x 8 grid will reveal the Hidden Pixel Art. Once the VR Robot has traveled every square, use the Reveal Answer button to check your solution.

Level 2: In VEXcode VR, create a 2D List with 8 rows and 8 columns. Program the VR Robot to navigate across the Hidden Pixel Art Playground. While the VR Robot is driving, record the data from the Hidden Pixel Art in the 2D List. Once the VR Robot has navigated around the entire Playground surface under the gold colored roof, use the Reveal Answer button to check your solution.

Level 3: Building from the Level 2 project, extend your project to display a representation of the Hidden Pixel Art using data from the 2D List to the Print Console. Once the VR Robot has navigated around the entire Playground surface under the gold colored roof, use the Reveal Answer button to check your solution.

 

Hints

  • To choose a puzzle, select the Starting Location button. 

  • The solution can be found using the Reveal Answer button after the VR Robot has navigated around the entire Playground surface under the gold colored roof.

  • Monitor the data in your 2D List in real time using the Monitor Console. 

  • Display a representation of the Hidden Pixel Art from the 2D list using the Print Console.

3.18 UI

Syllabus
Design, develop and implement a user interface (UI) to control a mechatronic system

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • be able to design, develop, and implement a user interface (UI) to control a mechatronic system.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • design a user interface that is intuitive and user-friendly for controlling a mechatronic system.
  • develop the UI using appropriate software tools and programming languages.
  • implement the UI to effectively control various functions and components of the mechatronic system.

  Content

The integration of User Interface (UI) in robotics marks a significant advancement in the way humans interact with machines. A well-designed UI is pivotal in enhancing the functionality, efficiency, and safety of robots, making them more accessible and effective for a variety of applications. This essay delves into the myriad ways UI is utilised in robotics, highlighting its critical importance.

 

Control Interfaces

One of the fundamental applications of UI in robotics is in control interfaces. These interfaces allow users to directly manipulate and control robotic systems.

  • Manual control interfaces, such as joysticks and touch screens, enable operators to guide robots in performing precise tasks. For instance, in manufacturing, robots are often manually controlled to assemble intricate components.
  • Teleoperation interfaces extend this capability to remote locations. Such systems are indispensable in environments where direct human intervention is risky or impossible, such as space exploration, underwater missions, or disaster response scenarios.

 

Monitoring and Feedback

Effective monitoring and real-time feedback are crucial for the efficient operation of robots.

  • Dashboard displays are essential UI components that provide real-time data on robot status, performance metrics, and diagnostics. These dashboards enable operators to monitor multiple robots simultaneously, ensuring they operate within optimal parameters.
  • Visual feedback through integrated cameras and sensors further enhances situational awareness, allowing operators to make informed decisions based on real-time imagery and sensor data. This is particularly vital in precision tasks such as robotic surgery or detailed assembly processes.

User Experience (UX)

The success of robotic systems heavily relies on the user experience (UX) offered by their UIs.

  • Intuitive design is paramount, ensuring that interfaces are user-friendly and reduce the learning curve for new users. For instance, in healthcare, robots assist in patient care, and the UI must be straightforward enough for medical staff to use without extensive training.
  • Haptic feedback adds another layer of interaction, providing tactile sensations that enhance control, especially in teleoperation scenarios. This feedback can simulate the sense of touch, allowing operators to feel the environment the robot is interacting with, thus improving precision and control.

Safety and Compliance

Ensuring safety is a critical aspect of robotics, and UIs play a crucial role in this domain.

  • Emergency stop and safety protocols are integrated into UIs to provide quick and reliable methods to halt robot operations in case of emergencies. This is essential in environments where humans and robots work in close proximity, such as in collaborative robotics in manufacturing.
  • Compliance and monitoring interfaces ensure that robots operate within predefined safety parameters, adhering to industry standards and regulations. These interfaces help in monitoring robot behaviour and implementing corrective measures when deviations occur.

 

Case Study: NASA

In all systems that involve interactions between humans and machines, the element that defines the quality of that interaction is the human/machine interface, also known as the user interface. A graphical user interface (GUI) can make the human interaction more engaging and intuitive, constrain user inputs to valid ranges and units, supply tabular and plot-based output where needed, and provide users with data from sensors on the robots that are needed for control.

JPL Robotics has created a number of very successful user interfaces tailored to the robotic systems being controlled. These robots have ranged from multi-arm manipulators for microgravity deployment or terrestrial surgical applications, to legged prototype-rovers for rough terrains, to multi-wheeled rovers including flight systems such as the Mars Pathfinder Sojourner Rover, the Mars Exploration Rovers (MER), Spirit and Opportunity, the Phoenix Lander, the Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) rover Curiosity, and the current Mars 2020 (M2020) rover and Helicopter, Perseverance and Ingenuity.

 

Key Interfaces Developed at JPL:

  1. RSVP (Robot Sequencing and Visualisation Program)

    • Used for all surface operations in Mars missions since 1997.
    • Creates all command sequences for robotic operations sent to Mars rovers and landers.
    • Tools within RSVP:
      • RoSE (Rover Sequence Editor): Supports all commands in the mission-command dictionary and interfaces with simulation tools.
      • HyperDrive: Provides multiple 3D graphics interfaces to stereo images and 3D terrain-model data for planning rover motions.
      • ArmSketch: Visual sequencing tool for generating arm sequences with optimised path and collision avoidance.
      • MobSketch: Visual sequencing tool for generating drive sequences.
      • ROCS (Robotic Operations and Computational Services): Provides stateless, RESTful API for rover simulation, planning, and operations.

  2. SSim (Surface Simulation)

    • Flight-software-in-the-loop simulation software predicting rover command outcomes before uplink to Mars.
    • Supports quick iteration of command development by rover planners.
    • Takes inputs like rover command sequences, terrain models, and rover memory state to output motion history and command durations.
    • Used in both MSL and M2020 for sequence validation and verification.

  3. Honeycomb 3D Visualisation Platform

    • General, web-based 3D visualisation platform for understanding robotic systems from development to operations.
    • Used in Mars 2020 for visualising autonomy products from the enhanced driving navigation system.
    • Displays flight products during autonomous driving to help operators understand and debug the process.
    • Allows toggling of displays, timeline scrubbing, and interaction with 3D views to analyze rover decisions.
    • Planned for expansion to other missions.

 

Applications and Impact:

  • RSVP: Critical for planning and executing complex rover missions, enabling precise control and movement on Mars.
  • SSim: Enhances mission success by simulating and validating commands, ensuring accurate and reliable rover operations.
  • Honeycomb: Improves understanding of autonomous driving decisions, facilitating mission planning and execution.

 

    Sources

  • Davis, S. (2024). Software engineering: The year 11 course (S. Davis, Ed.). Parramatta Education Centre.
  • https://www-robotics.jpl.nasa.gov/what-we-do/applications/user-interfaces/

3.19 Unit Tests

Syllabus
Create and use unit tests to determine the effectiveness and repeatability of each component’s control algorithm

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • be able to create and use unit tests to determine the effectiveness and repeatability of each component’s control algorithm in a mechatronic system.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • write unit tests for control algorithms of various components within a mechatronic system.
  • use these unit tests to evaluate the effectiveness and accuracy of the control algorithms.
  • analyse the results of the unit tests to identify any inconsistencies or errors in the control algorithms.
  • demonstrate the ability to refine and improve control algorithms based on the outcomes of the unit tests.

  Content

In control systems, ensuring that individual components operate effectively and consistently is critical for overall system performance. Unit testing plays a key role in achieving this by isolating and evaluating each component's control algorithm. By systematically testing these algorithms, we can verify their accuracy, detect potential errors, and ensure they produce repeatable results under various conditions. This page explores the importance of unit tests, provides steps to create them, and highlights their role in improving the reliability and precision of control systems.

 

What are Unit Tests?

Unit tests are a type of software testing that focus on individual components or modules of a system to determine whether they function as expected. In the context of control algorithms:

  • A unit refers to a single component or section of the control system.
  • The goal is to verify that the control algorithm performs correctly under specific conditions.

Unit testing ensures:

  1. Effectiveness – The control algorithm works as designed and produces the expected outcome.
  2. Repeatability – The algorithm produces consistent results when tested repeatedly under the same conditions.

 

Why are Unit Tests Important?

Unit testing is critical for the development and maintenance of control algorithms because it:

  • Detects errors early, reducing the cost and time of fixing issues.
  • Ensures that individual components work as expected before integrating them into larger systems.
  • Provides confidence that changes to the system do not break existing functionality.
  • Validates the accuracy, consistency, and performance of control algorithms.

In control systems, where precision and reliability are essential, unit tests help confirm that a component can handle real-world inputs effectively.

 

Creating Unit Tests

 

Define Test Scenarios

  • Identify expected inputs and outputs for the component.
  • Consider edge cases (e.g., maximum or minimum values, unexpected inputs, or boundary conditions).

For example:

Test Input (Scenario) Expected Output
Component input = 0 Control output = 0
Component input = 100 Control output = expected max
Component input = invalid data Control output = error handled

Write the Unit Tests

Write code or instructions that:

  1. Input specific test values into the control algorithm.
  2. Check the actual output against the expected output.

Test Repeatability

  • Run each test multiple times to check for consistent results.
  • Record and compare outputs to ensure the algorithm behaves reliably.

Evaluate Test Results

  • Analyse discrepancies between expected and actual outputs.
  • Document and address any issues found.

 

Example: Unit Test for a Control Algorithm

Scenario: A temperature control algorithm adjusts the output power to maintain a desired temperature.

Test Input Expected Output Pass/Fail
Target Temp = 20°C Output = Stable at 20°C Pass
Target Temp = 100°C Output = Max Power Pass
Target Temp = -10°C Output = Min Power Pass
Sensor Error/Invalid Output = Error Handling Pass

 

Key Considerations for Effective Unit Testing

  • Test Coverage: Ensure you test a wide range of conditions, including normal, edge, and error cases.
  • Automation: Use tools or software frameworks to automate tests for efficiency.
  • Consistency: Repeated tests must produce consistent results for reliability.
  • Documentation: Clearly document your test scenarios, expected outcomes, and any issues encountered.

 

    Sources

  • Davis, S. (2024). Software engineering: The year 11 course (S. Davis, Ed.). Parramatta Education Centre.

Build a Design

▶ Video won't play offline. Watch on Canvas · all modules
https://www.youtube.com/embed/gZQI1Z_viNg?si=tLi32WSaNKvOJ4Ln

Test Variations

Like all planes, paper aeroplanes experience four forces: gravity, thrust, lift, and drag. Simple changes, like wing size, body weight, and throw power, can significantly alter the forces your plane experiences.

Get creative and adjust various aspects of your plane. Here are a few ideas to get you started:

#1: Increase Lift

As the plane travels, air moves quickly over the top of the wings. This creates lower pressure over the wings, allowing the high pressure under the wings to lift the plane. Try making wider wings or wings that curve up or down at the ends.

#2: Limit Drag

Air molecules push against the front of the plane as it travels, slowing it down. Ensure your plane's nose is pointed, and the body is lightweight.

#3: Change The Thrust

When you throw your plane, you provide thrust, which pushes the plane forward through the air. This forward movement causes air molecules to travel over the top and bottom of the wings. Does the strength or angle at which you throw your plan impact it?

#4: Try A New Material

The weight of the plane can pull it downward. How does a heavier or lighter paper change your plane?

Structure Chart

Scenario:

You've been tasked with architecting the software backbone for a cutting-edge house security system. The system aims to ensure the safety of residents by monitoring various sensors deployed throughout the house and responding promptly to security events. It should detect intrusions, fire alarms, gas leaks, and other environmental hazards, provide real-time alerts, and enable quick emergency responses.

Question:

Develop a hierarchical structure chart outlining the main modules and their interactions for this house security system.

Structure Chart:

  1. Sensor Monitoring Module:

    • Responsible for continuously monitoring sensors installed throughout the house, including motion sensors, door/window sensors, smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors, and temperature sensors.

  2. Event Detection Module:

    • Analyses data received from the Sensor Monitoring Module to detect security events such as intrusions, fire alarms, gas leaks, and other environmental hazards.
    • Passes detected events to the Alarm Management Module for further processing.

  3. Alarm Management Module:

    • Receives security events from the Event Detection Module and determines the appropriate response based on predefined rules and user configurations.
    • Manages the activation and deactivation of alarms, including sirens, lights, and notifications to the user.
    • Passes control signals to the Emergency Response Module for immediate action if necessary.

  4. User Interface Module:

    • Provides a user-friendly interface for homeowners to interact with the security system.
    • Allows users to view sensor statuses, configure system settings, and receive real-time alerts.
    • Passes user commands and configurations to relevant modules for execution.

  5. System Configuration Module:

    • Enables users to customise system settings, including sensor sensitivity, alarm thresholds, and emergency contact information.
    • Stores and manages user preferences and configurations for the security system.

  6. Emergency Response Module:

    • Activates emergency protocols and notifies authorities (police, fire department, medical services) in case of verified security events requiring immediate intervention.
    • Receives signals from the Alarm Management Module to initiate emergency response procedures.

Interactions:

  • The Sensor Monitoring Module continuously collects data from sensors deployed throughout the house and passes it to the Event Detection Module.
  • The Event Detection Module analyses sensor data to detect security events and forwards detected events to the Alarm Management Module.
  • The Alarm Management Module determines the appropriate response to security events based on predefined rules and user configurations, activating alarms and notifying users as necessary.
  • The User Interface Module provides a platform for users to interact with the system, allowing them to view sensor statuses, configure settings, and receive alerts.
  • The System Configuration Module enables users to customise system settings and preferences, storing and managing user configurations.
  • The Emergency Response Module initiates emergency protocols and notifies authorities if verified security events require immediate intervention.

This structure chart outlines the main modules and their interactions within the house security system, facilitating efficient data flow and decision-making processes to ensure the safety and security of residents.

 

Criteria

Completeness Includes all essential modules and their interactions. The chart correctly identifies and depicts all essential modules and their interactions. The chart correctly identifies and depicts the most essential modules and their interactions. Some essential modules and their interactions are missing or inaccurately depicted in the chart. Many essential modules and their interactions are missing or inaccurately depicted in the chart. 2

Most modules are correctly identified, and their interactions are accurately depicted, with minor errors. Some modules are incorrectly identified, or their interactions are inaccurately depicted. Many modules are incorrectly identified, or their interactions are inaccurately depicted. 2

The structure chart is self-explanatory, well-organised, and effectively communicates the system architecture, enhancing understanding. The structure chart is clear and well-organised and effectively communicates the system architecture. The structure chart is somewhat clear and organised but may have minor issues in communication. Pseudocode

Instantiate an array of 20 entries and prompt the user to enter numbers in it. Once the array is filled, you must run a subroutine that checks for duplicate numbers and removes them from the array. You must then prompt the user to enter new numbers until there are no duplicates in the array. Use syntactically and logically correct Pseudocode to write this algorithm.
