Question: Draw a class diagram to represent the proposed calendar app. (4 marks)

Step 1. Read the question carefully

When reading the question, it's important to ask these two questions:

  1. What is the topic/content area? This question is testing our ability to create a class diagram for a calendar app. Class diagrams can be found on page 9 of your course specifications. Revise 4.11 Modelling Tools for more information or your year 11 "The object-orientated paradigm" topic.
  2. What are we required to do? We need to draw a class diagram, specifically, one that represents the proposed calendar app, so we now know that all our information is going to come from the requirements in the stimulus.

Stimulus:

A new calendar app is being created in an OOP language and the following requirements have been discovered.

  • A user can add many calendars but gets one by default when they open the app.
  • A user can add a range of items to their calendars, but an item can only belong to one calendar. These items include events, tasks, meetings, and recurring events.
  • All items have a start date/time and end date/time. They also have the ability to notify a user a certain time before they start. In addition to this, tasks have a status, recurring events have a recurrence type (e.g weekly/fortnightly, etc), and meetings have attendees.
  • A user can also view and delete items from a calendar or delete/view an entire calendar they’ve added themselves, but they must always have at least one calendar.

Step 2. Analyse the stimulus

When reading the stimulus, it's crucial that you highlight the important pieces of information so you don't leave anything out or have to go looking through a long stimulus. Here I've highlighted the classes in red, the hints about the relationships/inheritance/multiplicity in yellow, and the attributes/methods in blue.

Classes:

  • User
  • Calendar
  • Items (which we will rename calendar_items for clarity)
    • events
    • tasks
    • meetings
    • recurring events

Relationships:

  • Users have Calendars (1 to many calendars) We will make the assumption that a calendar can only belong to one user.
  • A calendar has calendar_items (0 to many calendar_items for each calendar). The stimulus specifies that a calendar_item can only belong to one calendar.
  • There is an inheritance relationship between calendar_items and all the different calendar_items (events, tasks, meetings, and recurring events). If you're even confused think, if this class is a type of another class, it would be inheritance but if a class belongs to or has some other class, then it is a relationship.
  • There also needs to be a relationship between User and Meetings. This one is harder to catch, but it is required because a meeting can have multiple users and each of those users need to be able to see their meetings. Even though the creator of the meeting can see their meeting through the calendar and calendar_item relationships, other user will not be able to without this extra relationship. The multiplicity is 1 to many on the meeting since a meeting needs to have one person and 0 to many on the meeting since a user may have 0 to many meetings.

Attributes/Methods:

Class Attributes Methods
User No explicit information on the attributes of a user have been mentioned so we just need to put ourselves in the shoes of the scenario and think, if we were developing a calendar app, what attributes would a user have? Logically the classics you can always fall back on are firstName, lastName and userID, though any reasonable attributes would be okay. The user needs to be able to add, view and delete calendars so the methods all be addCalendar(), deleteCalendar(), and viewCalendar().
Calendar No explicit information has been provided in the stimulus, so we will need to infer reasonable attributes. If you're struggling, think to a time you've used a calendar app and think. It must have a name and dateAdded is always a good filler if you can't think of any other attributes. Colour would be another good attribute since many calendar apps allow you to customise the colour of different calendars. We need to be able to add, view, and delete items on a calendar. Since these functions are directly associated with the feature of a calendar we will put them here. We need addCalendarItem(), viewCalendarItem, and deleteCalendarItem()
Calendar_Item

We are told that calendar item needs to have a start and end date and also be able to notify Users, so we will include a notify_time attribute. Since reminds usually give users an option from 5 mins or 10 mins before, the notify_time attribute will just be an integer which stores this value.

 To notify users, there will need to be a notify method.
Event

Event will inherit all the properties from Calendar_Item and I can't think of any extra attributes to add, so it's perfectly okay to leave it blank.

 Event will inherit the notify method, and we don't need any extras so we can leave it empty too.
Task

Task It will inherit all the properties from Calendar_Item. However we need to add an extra status property. This status will be stored as an int. A string could also work, but an int is more robust. E.g 0 = not started, 1 = in progress and 2 = done, etc.

 Task will inherit the notify method, and we don't need any extras so we can leave it empty too.
Meeting

We have a relationship which will encode who the meeting attendees are, but just for added clarity we will include attendees as an attribute and the data type will be an array of User objects.

 We need a method to start and end the meeting as the very least.
Recurring Event

We need to store the recurrence type, eg. weekly, fortnightly and store it as an int e.g 0 =  daily, 1 = weekly etc.

 We need a manage_recurrence() method to schedule/render all the recurrences when the item is added to the calendar.

Note that you will be thinking through everything in this table as you highlight the stimulus. You can use a table like this to help you plan, but you have limited time in the exam, so it's best to just highlight the stimulus.

Step 3.1 Draw the Classes in the Class Diagram

  1. Click the library icon at the top right of the drawing area to open the shape library.
  2. Select the class diagram shape to insert it into the canvas. Note that this is a composite shape. It's just a set of lines grouped together. If you want to resize the shape (e.g to add more space for attribute) you just need to right click the shape and select "Ungroup selection" or select the shape, scroll to the bottom of the sidebar and in the "actions" section, click the ungroup button.
  3. Use the text tool to add a title in the top row of the shape. Then add the attributes in the second row and methods in the last row. It's perfectly okay to leave sections empty (link in Event) if it makes sense in the context of the scenario.
  4. Duplicate the class and update each duplicate with the information for all the other classes.
  5. Try and arrange your diagram so lines don't cross. E.g have all child class below the parent and related classes next to each other.

Step 3.2. Draw the connections

  1. Use the arrow tool to draw a the relationships and inheritance between the classes. Recall that relationships use unfilled arrows and inheritance uses filled arrows. You can set the arrow heads by clicking on the arrow an navigating to the arrowheads section in the drawing tool sidebar and set the type of arrow (including none) for each side of the arrow.
  2. If you have added a relationship, use the text tool to add a word on the arrow that indicates the type of relationship such as "has", "studies", "uses", etc.
  3. Add the multiplicity on each side of the arrow. There are a range of multiplicity options. Use the one that makes more logical sense from your analysis of the stimulus. Also remember that the multiplicity as attributed to the class it is closest to, e.g in the diagram below, the 1..1 next to the User class means there can only be one user mapping to a calendar and the 1..* next to the Calendar class means that 1 to many calendars can map to a User, so together they reveal that a User can have as many calendars as they want, as long as they have one and those calendar can only belong to that one User. The inheritance arrows don't have multiplicities.

Step 4. Examine your work and make sure it's correct

Our diagram has all the classes is needs, it has fully featured attributes and methods (including ones we created ourselves based on the scenario) and all the links have been made appropriately. The last thing to glance at would be the multiplicities to make sure you haven't mistyped one of them. This is a common mistake, so double check.

 

Marking Criteria (through the eyes of a marker)

How to get full marks?

  • To get full marks you need to create a substantially correct class diagram. This means that if one of your relationships was a bit off (e.g if you didn't include the relationship from Users to Meetings and just went with the attendees attribute storing the User object being enough, that would be substantially correct. Likewise, if you missed one of the non essential attributes, that would still be considered substantially correct. However, besides that, you need to have all the suitable classes kitted out with attributes, methods and have the correct arrows/multiplicities on the whole.
  • Know how to create class diagrams. Revise 4.11 Modelling Tools for more information or your year 11 "The object-orientated paradigm" topic. Also revise page 9 of your course specifications.

I'm completely stuck and not getting anywhere. How do I salvage as many marks as a I can?

  • Don't leave the question blank. If you're totally stuck, there are always some basic things you can do to guarantee at least one or two marks. E.g there is one mark for "showing some understanding of the scenario". After this, flag the question so you can come back to it after you finish the rest of the exam, hopefully with fresh ideas to claim a few more marks.
  • Providing something that resembles a class diagram with some words from the stimulus would get you one mark and if you were just able to show the relationship between Users, Calendars, and Calendar_Items or just the inheritance between Calendar_Items and the children, that would be two marks. If you are total stuck, try making a table like in Step 2 above and use that a guide to build your class diagram and even if it's not perfect, you should land 3 marks.

Decision Trees

Drawing Questions — Decision Tree

Decision trees are composed of a series of question in rectangles attached to a series of possible answers that link into further questions below. There is a path from the root of the tree all the way to every leaf based on the answered made to each question in the tree. They can go vertically down the page or horizontally across the page. Below is an example of a vertical decision tree. If you're not up to date on decision trees, revise page 10 of your course specifications.

Steps for Answering Decision Tree Questions:

  1. Read the question carefully to see what you have to do.
  2. Read and highlight the stimulus. Decision tree questions almost always have a stimulus. When you read the stimulus, you need to use the highlighter tool to highlight any clues to the questions you need to ask as well as what the end points (leaves) of the tree will be.
  3. Use the drawing tool to create your response. You always start with the root of the tree and decide how many different answers there are (binary selection or multiple) and make your way down the tree until you have all the required solutions/leaves.
  4. Reread the question/stimulus and make sure you haven't missed anything.

Question: Draw the decision tree to distinguish between the web protocols. (3 marks)

Step 1. Read the question carefully

When reading the question, it's important to ask these two questions:

  1. What is the topic/content area? This question is testing our ability to create a decision tree in the context of web protocols. Decision trees can be found on page 10 of your course specifications and web protocols are in your Programming for the Web topic under "Investigate and describe the function of web protocols and their ports". Revise 2.3 Web Protocols for more information.
  2. What are we required to do? We need to draw a decision tree that allows us to distinguish between web protocols. We will need to refer to the stimulus for the exact requirements.

Stimulus:

A student is interested in testing their knowledge of web protocols so they create a decision tree that can identify a protocol based on it’s characteristics.

The decision tree needs to allow someone distinguish between HTTP, HTTPS, POP, SMTP, and IMAP. It should ask appropriate yes/no questions about the protocol’s characteristics to arrive at a unique conclusion.

For example if a protocol is used for transferring web pages on the internet and runs on port 80, then it is HTTP. This could be one of the paths in the decision tree, but it also needs to account for the other protocols by asking appropriate questions and including appropriate pathways that end at a single protocol.

Step 2. Analyse the stimulus

The stimulus makes it clear that we need to make a decision tree that asks increasingly nuanced questions that allow us to differentiate between the five protocols mentioned. We also need to arrive at a unique conclusion, so we can have one branch that says it could be HTTP or HTTPS, we need to have a single protocol at the end of each pathway. Also, we can only ask yes/no questions so we can't just have one level with five branches that ask what port the protocol runs on and distinguish the protocols like that. Instead, we need to ask four yes no questions to adequately tell the five protocols apart.

For each question as we move down the tree, we need to think of a new more targeted characteristic that can allow us to separate the protocols from each other sort of like how we would use a decision tree to diagnose an illness — first we start broad like where the pain is or what the protocol is used for and get finer such as what type of pain is felt or what port the protocol runs on.

Step 3. Draw the decision tree

  1. Since we need to ask at least three questions before arriving at a conclusion, we will ask a broad question to begin with like 'what is the protocol used for'. To make this a yes or no question, we will use "Used for transferring webpage data." If this question is yes it could be either HTTP or HTTPS and if not, it could be SMTP, IMAP, or POP3.
  2. Now to differentiate between HTTP and HTTPS the we could use the port it runs on. If it runs on port 80 it is HTTPS and if not, it is HTTPS. We could also ask a question of if it is encrypted or not which is another valid characteristic. Now we have finished this side of the tree.
  3. Now we need to start differentiating between SMTP, IMAP, and POP3. To do this we need to find a characteristic that only one of the three has. In this case we will ask if the protocol is used to transfer mail between mail servers since only SMTP is used for this.
  4. Now we are only left with the branch that deals with IMAP and POP3. To distinguish between these we need another appropriate characteristic. We know that only IMAP is used to synchronise mail across devices while POP3 simply retrieves mail from the server to one device. So, we can ask weather the protocol is used to synchronise email across devices and if yes, it is IMAP and if no, it's POP3.

Step 4. Examine your work and make sure it's correct

Looking back to our highlights of the stimulus we have only used yes/no questions, all our branches end at single protocols, and all the questions use defining features of the protocols to accurately distinguish them. Therefore we can be fairly confident our answer is correct.

Marking Criteria (through the eyes of a marker)

How to get full marks?

  • To get full marks you need to provide a correct decision tree that uniquely distinguishes between all the protocols. This means each question needs to clearly and accurately divide the pool of protocols into smaller ones until we are only left with one clear result at the end of a brach of the decision tree. Highlighting the stimulus will help ensure you don't miss any of the key requirements.
  • Know how to create decision trees. Revise page 10 of your course specifications.

I'm completely stuck and not getting anywhere. How do I salvage as many marks as a I can?

  • Don't leave the question blank. If you're totally stuck, there are always some basic things you can do to guarantee at least one or two marks. E.g there is one mark for "showing some understanding of decision trees". This means you just need to put down one question with a yes and no leading into two results and that would get you one mark. After this, flag the question so you can come back to it after you finish the rest of the exam, hopefully with fresh ideas to claim a few more marks.
  • Even if you're not sure how to differentiate between the protocols, try and do the broader questions at the top of the tree and you may get enough correct so that you sit in the two mark range where up to two questions can be wrong.

Structure Chart

Drawing Questions — Structure Chart

Structure charts represent a system by showing the separate subroutines that make up the system and their relationship to each other. They show the hierarchy of a program including which subroutines work together to produce a particular result and the data/flags passed between them all. They show the order in which modules/submodules are called since they are read from left to right top to bottom and there can be repetition and selection using appropriate symbols. Another sub tasks go down the diagram and any distinct steps of a process go across the diagram. If you're not up to date on structure charts, revise page 7 of your course specifications.

The image below is from page 7 of your course specs and it is not a good example of a structure chart.

  • Firstly, all subroutines that are on the same level must be in line with each other, however the example in your course specs has them all over the place.
  • They also have data and flags going down and up on inconsistent sides of the line. Stuff going down into a subroutine goes on the left of the connecting line and stuff coming up out of the subroutine goes on the right of the connecting line.
  • Also, connecting lines should all start at the bottom centre of the parent node and connect to the top centre of the child node for consistency and neatness. This is not adhered to in the course specs.
  • Other than that, the symbols are correct and the logic is okay.

Steps for Answering Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD) Questions:

  1. Read the question carefully to see what you have to do.
  2. Read and highlight the stimulus. Structure chart questions almost always have a stimulus. When you read the stimulus, you need to use the highlighter tool to highlight any clues to what the modules are, their hierarchy and what data/flags/repetition/decision you will need.
  3. Use the drawing tool to create your structure chart. 
    1. Draw the modules and arrange them in their hierarchy and leave enough space so data/flags can be placed along side the connecting lines.
    2. Draw all the data/flags/repetition/decisions.
  4. Reread the question/stimulus and make sure you haven't missed anything.

Question: Draw a structure chart to represent this home automation system. (4 marks)

Step 1. Read the question carefully

When reading the question, it's important to ask these two questions:

  1. What is the topic/content area? This question is testing our ability to create an structure chart. They can be found on page 7 of your course specifications.
  2. What are we required to do? We need to draw a structure chart that represents the home automation system in the stimulus.

Stimulus:

A home automation system uses a variety or sensors and actuators to automate home functions such as turning on lights, arming alarms, and locking/unlocking doors.

The central computer monitors all sensor inputs and then processes the sensor input. Depending on the analysis of the sensor values, certain actions are completed. E.g if motion is detected in a room, the lights will be turned on. After 9PM, the door automatically lock and if the motion sensors are triggers while the system is armed, an alarm will go off a the home owners will have a text message sent to them.

There is a web dashboard which is used to control the system such as sensor sensitivity and what times the door lock / alarm is armed.

Step 2. Analyse the stimulus

As you read the stimulus, highlight any processes/ subroutines you see and also the data/flags/repetition/decisions.

Subroutines

In the second paragraph of the stimulus, we can see the first subroutine is probably "get sensor values" followed by "process sensor value". Then there will be a bunch of actions that need to happen based on that data analysis. The examples in the second sentence of the second paragraph indicate the need for "manage lights" and "lock/unlock doors", and "manage alarm system".

Now it also mentioned setting off an alarm and messaging the home owners. We need to decide if these go on the same level as "get sensor values" and "manage alarm system" or if they are subprocesses of an exisiting subroutine we've identified, and indeed they can definitely fit as subprocesses of the "manage alarm system" subroutine. This is because the stimulus said  that while the system is armed, if motion is detected, the alarm is set off and the home owners are contacted and this is all part of the alarm system. Now these two happen in an order, first the alarm is set off, and then the home owners are sent a message, so the "set off alarm" sub process will be below the "manage alarm system" subroutine but going to the left and "message owner" will be below "manage alarm system" too, but to the right of "set off alarm" since it happens only after the alarm is actually set off. Then the process "manage alarm system" is able to coordinate these two subprocesses based on the data/flags it receives.

Finally, it also mentioned a web dashboard which allows settings to be adjusted. This means we need subroutine for adjusting settings. This will be on the same level as all the other main processes since it's a distinct step in the home automation system rather than a subprocess or an exisiting subroutine.

Data/Flags/Decisions

Subroutine Input Output
get sensor values sensor settings as data which are passed up from the "configure smart home settings" and back down the the "get sensor values" process Sensor readings (including the time) as data since a clock is sort of a type of sensor.
analyse sensor data Sensor readings as data MotionDetected as a flag. There will obviously be data/flags returned, but for the functionality described in the stimulus, this is enough.
manage alarm system

motion detected as a flag

isArmed as a flag (isArmed is considered to be part of the configure smart home settings and is selectively passed down from the parent module "home automation system" which coordinates all submodules.)

 alarmActive as a flag (not used for much, but still important to return something relevant.)
lock/unlock doors

time as data

doorSettings as data (so it knows when to lock and unlock doors)

 doorsLocked as a flag so the system knows the state of the doors.
Manage lights

motionDetected as flag

 lightsOn as flag so the system knows if the the lights are on or not.
configure smart home settings

current settings as data passed down form the parent module "home automation system" which stores /passes the settings around.

 newSettings as data after they have been edited by the user.
set off alarm

motionDetected as flag

isArmed as flag

The decision diamond tells us that we only take this branch if both of the flags are true.

 alarmActive as a flag so we know weather to send the home owners a message.
message owner

alarmActive as flag

The decision diamond tells us that we only take this branch is alarmActive is true.

 success as a flag so the system know the message was sent correctly.

Repetition

Since we want to constantly monitor the sensors, complete the action and be able to update the settings any time, we need all of the processes on level 1 of the diagram to be looped.

Step 3.1 Draw the modules and arrange them in their hierarchy

  1. First, we need to insert a rectangle and inside place some text that says "home automation system". This will be the top (level 0) of our diagram.
  2. Then we add all the level 1 subroutines and make sure the are spaced far enough apart and far enough below level 0 so when we add the data/flags, they fit.
  3. Now add the level 2 subroutines below "manage alarm system" and place them below, the same distance from level 1 as level 1 is from level 0. Everything should be aligned properly.
  4. Add the lines between everything and make sure it looks like there is enough space. If not, move stuff around.

Step 3.2 Draw all the data/flags/repetition/decisions.

  1. Open the shape library and you'll see the structure chart diamond, repetition, data, and flag shapes. They are below.
  2. Always make sure data/flags go down of the left side of the line and come up on the right side of the line.
  3. Use the text tool the label the data/flags.
  4. Add the repetition symbol at the top over all the level one processes.
  5. Add the diamond decisions at the bottom for the "set off alarm" and "message owner" processes.

Step 4. Examine your work and make sure it's correct

Looking back to our highlights of the stimulus we can see we've included all the required functionality and added a great deal of our own interpretation to make the diagram better. All the data/flags make sense are are positioned on the correct sides of the connecting lines. Everything is neatly aligned.

Marking Criteria (through the eyes of a marker)

How to get full marks?

  • To get full marks, you need to create a "substantially correct entity relationship diagram" that includes all the core processes, flags, data, repetition, and decisions. When we analysed the stimulus, we made sure we were aware of all the processes needed and we also planned all the data/flags, repetition and decision. Even if we missed one small detail, we could still be "substantially correct" and get full marks, but by being rigorous and not just relying on our memory we can reduce the number of silly mistakes whist also improving our understanding of the question and quality of our solution.
  • Know how to create structure charts. Revise page 7 of your course specifications.

I'm completely stuck and not getting anywhere. How do I salvage as many marks as a I can?

  • Don't leave the question blank. If you're totally stuck, there are always some basic things you can do to guarantee at least one or two marks. E.g there is one mark for "providing a diagram that shows some understanding of the scenario". This means you just need to put down some of the subroutines.
  • Even if you're not totally sure about something, just give it a go and you might be right. E.g even if you don't exactly how to arrange all the subroutines if you include as many as you can and attach appropriate data, you can still get 2 to 3 marks.

Entity Relationship Diagram

Drawing Questions — Entity Relationship Diagrams (ERD)

An entity relationship diagram (sometimes called a database schema) is used to represent the tables and relationships in a relational database. They use rectangles to represent the tables with the table's title at the top and separate from the attributes below via a dividing line. These attributes are all the fields in each record of the table and include the primary and foreign keys of the table. Lines are drawn between them and labeled with the nature of the relationship. See the example below from your course specs. If you're not up to date on entity relationship diagrams, revise page 23 of your course specifications.

Steps for Answering Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD) Questions:

  1. Read the question carefully to see what you have to do.
  2. Read and highlight the stimulus. Decision tree questions almost always have a stimulus. When you read the stimulus, you need to use the highlighter tool to highlight any clues to the questions you need to ask as well as what the end points (leaves) of the tree will be.
  3. Use the drawing tool to create your ERD. 
    1. Draw the tables with the table title, attributes and labeled primary keys (P) and foreign keys (F).
    2. Draw the links between the tables and label them with the multiplicity.
  4. Reread the question/stimulus and make sure you haven't missed anything.

Question: Draw an entity relationship diagram to represent the proposed calendar app. (4 marks)

Step 1. Read the question carefully

When reading the question, it's important to ask these two questions:

  1. What is the topic/content area? This question is testing our ability to create an entity relationship diagram. Entity relationship diagrams can be found on page 23 of your course specifications. Revise 2.3 Web Protocols for more information.
  2. What are we required to do? We need to draw a decision tree that allows us to distinguish between web protocols. We will need to refer to the stimulus for the exact requirements.

Stimulus:

A new website calendar app is being created for a learning management system and the following requirements have been identified:

  1. A user can add many calendars to their account.
  2. A user can add a range of items to their calendars, but an item can only belong to one calendar. These items include
    • events (start date/time, end date/time, description).
    • tasks (due date, duration, description, priority, status).
    • meetings (start date/time, end date/time, has other users as attendees who can also see the meeting on their calendar).

The following tables have been identified for the schema

  • Users
  • Calendars
  • Events
  • Tasks
  • Meetings
  • Meeting_Attendees

Step 2. Analyse the stimulus

As you read the stimulus, highlight any tables you identify as red, any attributes in blue, and any clues as to the relationships between the tables in yellow.

Tables

In the stimulus above, the question has been kind enough to give us all the tables we need, although even with out it, there is enough information in the main part of the stimulus to identify these. The tables we need are Users, Calendars, Events, Tasks, Meetings and Meeting_Attendees. Meeting_Attendees is an intermediary table which allows there to be a many to many relationship between Users and Meetings.

Relationships

  • Since users can have multiple calendars there will be a one-to-many relationship between Users and Calendars.
  • Since calendars can have many events, tasks and meetings, there will be a one to many relationship between Calendars and all these tables.
  • In the stimulus, the description for the meetings table is that it "has other users as attendees who also see the meeting on their calendar." This gives us a hint that the attendees are not merely stored as an attribute in the meetings table, but rather, there is a many to many relationship between Users and Meetings where all users are linked to and can see their meetings and multiple meetings can be linked to a User. This explains the presence of the  Meeting_Attendees table which is an intermediary table between Users and Meetings to allow this many-to-many relationship.

Attributes

Now that we know the relationship we also know the primary and foreign keys needed for each tables along with their other attributes.

  • Below some of the attributes are in green font. These are the I've added to relate to the scenario better and fill in the gaps of the stimulus.
  • The primary and foreign keys we've derived from the stimulus a in orange font.
  • The provided attributes form the stimulus are in black font.
Table Attributes
Users userId (P), firstName, lastName, dateJoined
Calendars calendarId (P), name, colour, dateAdded, userId (F)
Events eventId (P), startDateTime, endDateTime, description, calendarId (F)
Tasks taskId (P), dueDate, duration, description, priority, status, calendarId (F)
Meetings meetingId (P), startDateTime, endDateTime, calendarId (F)
Meeting_Attendees meeting_attendeeId (P), meetingId (F), userId (F)

Now we are ready to draw our ERD.

Step 3.1 Draw the tables with their attributes.

  1. First, we need to insert a table item. It looks like a two row table with the top part only large enough for a title and the lower part with plenty of space for all the attributes. You can find it by open by clicking on the "library" button at the top right of the drawing tool. Inside you will see the shape below. Click to insert it on your Canvas.
  2. Use the text tool to add the title of the table in the top row of the shape. Double click on the rectangle to customise the positioning of the text on it.
  3. Add another text box in the large portion below and add all the attributes making sure to include a (P) after primary keys and an (F) after foreign keys. If you need to resize the table shape, you need to right click on it and select "Ungroup selection". This will disassemble the shape into a rectangle and dividing line. You can now resize each part of the shape individually weather you need more width or height.

Step 3.2 Draw the relationships between the tables.

  1. Using the arrow tool (press A on your keyboard as a shortcut), draw a line from one table to the other making sure the line intersects the table's boarder at the height of the attribute the relationship is being made on. It's often a good idea to ensure the text box inside the table shape spans the width of the table so the arrows link consistently. 
  2. Select the arrow and then set the type of be "elbow arrow" from the "arrow type" section in the sidebar. This will make it from a curvy/straight arrow into one that makes right angle turns.
  3. Set the arrowheads of both sides of the arrow to none. This will make it look like a line, but we needed to use an arrow to get to "elbow" style often used in ERDs.
  4. Repeat step 1 adding the arrows between all the tables. You may find that you need to move some of the tables so the lines don't cross. We don't want to have crossing lines on ERDs if it's possible. Sometimes the arrow tool can be frustrating. Just make sure you start them right on the edge boarder of the shape and then let go when you are hovering over the destination for the line.
  5. Only after you've added all your lines should you add the multiplicities since we don't want to keep moving them around as we rearrange the diagram and it can also confuse the arrow tool making it produce all sorts of crazy results. To add a "1" use the text tool and type "1" into it. For the infinity symbol, open the library again and select the infinity symbol from the list of shapes. Once you've got one of each, you can just copy them to all the other lines.

Step 4. Examine your work and make sure it's correct

Looking back to our highlights of the stimulus we can see we've added all the required tables and attributes. We've also added a few of our own to add extra detail. We've also included all the correct relationships required.

Marking Criteria (through the eyes of a marker)

How to get full marks?

  • To get full marks, you need to create a "substantially correct entity relationship diagram" that includes all required tables/attributes, primary/foreign keys and relationships + multiplicities. To ensure we included all of these, we highlighted them stimulus. Even if we missed one small detail, we could still be "substantially correct" and get full marks, but by being rigorous and not just relying on our memory we can reduce the number of silly mistakes whist also improving our understanding of the question and quality of our solution.
  • Know how to create entity relationship diagrams. In this question, the hardest part with the many-to-many relationship involving the intermediary table. Revise page 23 of your course specifications.

I'm completely stuck and not getting anywhere. How do I salvage as many marks as a I can?

  • Don't leave the question blank. If you're totally stuck, there are always some basic things you can do to guarantee at least one or two marks. E.g there is one mark for "providing a diagram that shows some understanding of the scenario". This means you just need to put down one or two tables the have a title and some attributes and you would get one mark. If you had two correct tables and maybe a simple relationship, that could get you two marks which is better that none, so always put down what you know.
  • Even if you're not totally sure about something, just give it a go and you might be right. E.g even if you're not sure how to do the many to many relationship, just look at the relationships you've identified and the tables and try something that might work.

 Question Breakdown & Tips and Tricks

Question: Write the algorithm using pseudocode. Include at least one subroutine in your answer. (4 marks)
The array is called day_array and it is indexed from 1.

Step 1. Read the question carefully

When reading the question, it's important to ask these two questions:

  1. What is the topic/content area? This question is testing our ability to create algorithms and present them as pseudocode.
  2. What are we required to do? We are required to read the stimulus and write the algorithm described. We must ensure that we include at least one subroutine. We also get some crucial information regarding the name of the array we will be using and that it is indexed from 1.

Stimulus:

A company is developing a learning management system and wants to build an algorithm that will help schedule a student’s homework time to improve productivity.

A student’s day is represented as an array of records with a length of 48. This account for all the 30 minute time slots of a given day. Each record has a state which can be occupied or free. Slots that are free are empty and slots that are occupied have an ‘X’. The record also has a slot type which could be ‘H’ for homework, ‘S’ for school time, and ‘F’ for free time. Homework time can only be added to time slots that have a type “H”.

Your job is to write an algorithm that takes the number of homework slots a student would like to add to their schedule and see if it fits in their current day. If there is enough space, each homework time slot that is used should be filled with an ‘X”. The program should then return “Homework Added”.

If there is not enough space, it should return “Not enough space” followed by the number of extra homework slots required. E.g “Not enough space. 1 extra homework slot required”.

For example, if the array looked like the one below and the student wanted to add one homework slot, the program would add an X to the availability part of the record at index 32 and return “Homework Added”.


Step 2. Analyse the stimulus

You need to highlight everything you are told about the nature of the program. In this case everything we know about the array which stores the students daily schedule is highlighted in yellow.

Highlight what you need to make (in green above) and then all the requirements of the program (in blue above).

Array based question will sometimes include a diagram for you to aid in understanding the scenario.

Note that since we are working with an array of records, we can access each field of the record using the dot operator like day_array[i].type

Step 3. Write your mainline and decide on the subroutines you will use.

Figuring out the mainline will come primarily from our blue highlights since they define the different outputs and pathways our algorithm needs to have. We will also identify the subroutines we need as we write the mainline.

  1. The first thing the program needs to do is check the availability for adding a certain number of homework slots. We will use a check_space subroutine to see if there is space. This subroutine will return 0 if there is space and if there isn't, it will return the number of extra spaces required.
  2. Then if there is space, we need to add the set the slots of occupied and return "Homework Added". We will use a subroutine called assign_homework to set the homework slots of occupied.
  3. If there is no space, we send a message to the user with the number of extra slots required to meet the request.

These three requirements give us the following mainline.

BEGIN add_homework (slots)
        is_space = check_space (slots)
        IF is_space = 0 THEN
                assign_homework (slots)
                DISPLAY 'Homework Added'
        ELSE
                DISPLAY 'Not enough space. ' + is_space + 'extra homework slots required'.
        ENDIF
END add_homework (slots)

Note

The mainline is very simple, short, and un-cluttered. This is expected by the markers. You should not have your complicated, low-level logic in the mainline. The mainline should only contain a high-level overview that anyone could understand after reading it once. The subroutines it calls should do all the complex work.

Step 4. Write your subroutines.

 In step 3, we identified two subroutines. These were check_space and assign_homework.

check_space requires us to iterate over all the time slots of the day and count how many free homework slots we have. To keep track of the free homework slots we use a variable called slots_free and we increment it when we find an index of the array that is not occupied and has a type of 'H' for homework. We are using a while loop because we don't just want to blindly iterate over the entire array, but rather keep going until we find the required number. If we get to the end and still don't have the required number, then we can confirm there are not enough slots, but if we find enough early, we don't want to keep iterating over the rest of the array since that would be inefficient. 

assign_homework is used to set the availability of a certain number of homework slots being added by the user. Since we have already confirmed there are enough slots from the check_space subroutine, we can iterate over the array setting the availability of each homework slot to 'X' for however many we are adding.

Step 5. Reread the question and test the algorithm.

  1. Check  your pseudocode syntax. You need to make sure the every IF finishes with an ENDIF and every WHILE end with and ENDWHILE. Recall that FOR loops don't have a standard ending keyword, but instead uses NEXT variable after the code inside the loop. Also ensure each of your subroutines have an END subroutine_name (all parameters if any) including all the parameters it takes in, if any. Make sure all these key works are capitalised.
  2. Check for silly mistakes. Ensure that you haven't forgotten to increment any variables your are using for iteration. E.g don't forget to iterate count or slots_free in this question. 
  3. Check your logic. Test your subroutine in your head by passing in a value and running through it step by step to see what output you get. Make sure this is the correct output. If you subroutine has lots of cases, try values that lie on the edges of the cases to ensure all the pathways work as you expect.

 

Marking Criteria (through the eyes of a marker)

How to get full marks?

  1. The first key phrase is "substantially correct". This means, to get full marks, your algorithm doesn't have to be perfect. If you made one silly mistake like forgetting to increment on of the variables, you will likely still get full marks. Likewise, if you forget one ENDIF you still have a good chance of getting 4/4. That said, we are aiming to reduce the number of these errors so they don't add up.
  2. You need to practice a lot of different algorithm questions to get experience with different control structures and data types. There are lots of algorithm question  that can be found in past HSC papers of the old Software Design and Development syllabus.
  3. Make sure you highlight the stimulus so you don't miss anything important and know exactly what you are making.

I'm completely stuck and not getting anywhere. How do I salvage as many marks as a I can?

  • Don't leave the question blank. If you're totally stuck, there are always some basic things you can do to guarantee at least one or two marks. After this, flag the question so you can come back to it after you finish the rest of the exam, hopefully with fresh ideas to claim a few more marks.
  • The best thing you can do is start by laying out your mainline. Read the stimulus and question carefully and think about what a program might need to do at it's most simply level to achieve the desired result. Often times the question will explicitly state what you mainline needs to do. From there you can create subroutines for each of the things the mainline has to do.

Python Programming — Example Question (annotated answer with though process)

Sample Answer

 Question Breakdown & Tips and Tricks

Question: Write a python program that

  • Calculates the average band performance of all the students using the data above.
  • Calculates the average effort rating of the students using the data above.
  • Displays the average band and average effort rating to the output. The average effort rating should be to 2 decimal placed and the average band should be rounded to the nearest whole number.
  • Uses a function to calculate the band.

Step 1. Read the question carefully

When reading the question, it's important to ask these two questions:

  1. What is the topic/content area? This question is testing your python program writing skills. This is under the "Programming with Python" section of your course specs.
  2. What are we required to do? We need write a python program that calculates the average band from all the scores given in the array of dictionaries in the stimulus, calculates the average effort rating in the same way, displays these two to the output and also uses a function to calculate the band. This means the band calculation cannot be in our mainline.

Stimulus:

A school wants to develop a tool to help classes correlate their overall performance with the effort ratings of students. School report data has been placed in python as an array of dictionaries. The exact structure is as below:

students = [
{"name": "Student 1", "effort": 8, "score": 95},
{"name": "Student 2", "effort": 7, "score": 85},
{"name": "Student 3", "effort": 5, "score": 72},
{"name": "Student 4", "effort": 9, "score": 94},
{"name": "Student 5", "effort": 8, "score": 89},
{"name": "Student 6", "effort": 7, "score": 83},
{"name": "Student 7", "effort": 4, "score": 74},
{"name": "Student 8", "effort": 10, "score": 98},
{"name": "Student 9", "effort": 5, "score": 79},
{"name": "Student 10", "effort": 8, "score": 87}
]

Write a python program that

  • Calculates the average band performance of all the students using the data above.
  • Calculates the average effort rating of the students using the data above.
  • Displays the average band and average effort rating to the output. The average effort rating should be to 2 decimal placed and the average band should be rounded to the nearest whole number.
  • Uses a function to calculate the band.

Bands are calculated as follows:
Band 6 (90 – 100)
Band 5 (80 – 89)
Band 4 (70 – 79)
Band 3 (60 – 69)
Band 2 (50 – 59)
Band 1 (0 – 49)

Using the students array above, the output should look like:

Step 2. Analyse the stimulus

There is a lot to unpack in this stimulus.

  • We are given the data structure we will be operation on. We will just copy this into the Python code writing area when we start creating the program.
  • We are also told how to format the output numbers with the average band being the closest whole number and the average effort being to two decimal places.
  • We are also given the guidelines for how to calculate a band from a score. 
  • Finally, we are given a sample output which our program should also replicate in terms of output style and correct values.

Step 3. Draft your response quickly in your head.

Based on the stimulus, we know we need a function to calculate the band given a score so that will go at the top of the program. Then in our main line we will to calculate the averages. It would be wise to use a for loop to iterate over each student and add their band and effort rating to a running total which we can then divide by the number of students at the end to get the average. Finally, we would need to print the values to the output.

Step 4. Create your response using the online HSC python coding tool.

  1. First, copy the array into the input code section of the online HSC writing tool.
  2. Write the calcuate_band function using the conversion criteria provided in the stimulus.
  3. Write the mainline of the program
    1. Initialise the variables you are going to use to track the running totals
    2. Write a for loop that iterates over each student and use the dictionary key access syntax to extract the score and pass it into the calcuate_band function and add the to a running band total. Also extract the effort rating and it to a running total of effort ratings.
    3. After the loop, divide the running totals by the number of students, remembering the round the average_band to the nearest whole number using the round() function.
    4. Then we print out the values using the python f-string formatting syntax to print the average effort rating to 2 decimal places. You don't need to do any formatting for the band since it's already rounded to an integer in the division calculation.

Step 5. Examine your work and make sure it's correct

  1. Click "run" at the top right and make sure you output is identical to the sample output.
  2. Then glance over your code one more time to make sure there are no glaring logic issues such as using ">" instead of ">=".
  3. Add new lines to segment parts of the code the do different things for better readability.

 

Marking Criteria (through the eyes of a marker)

How to get full marks?

  1. The first key phrase is "substantially correct". This means, to get full marks, your code doesn't have to be perfect. If you missed one small thing, you can still get 6/6, so don't stress, just focus on doing your best job. E.g if there was one minor logic error in your band calculation you could very well still get full marks.
  2. The other key phrase is "including all the features". This means you need to complete each of the five dots points to a substantially correct quality. If you don't use a function to calculate band or you don't calculate one of the averages, you will only get 5 marks at most.

I'm completely stuck and not getting anywhere. How do I salvage as many marks as a I can?

  • Don't leave the question blank. If you're totally stuck, there are always some basic things you can do to guarantee at least one or two marks. After this, flag the question so you can come back to it after you finish the rest of the exam, hopefully with fresh ideas to claim a few more marks.
  • You'll notice there is one mark for "showing some understanding of the requirement". This means literally setting up some variables to track totals could get you one mark.
  • If you satisfy 2 or more of the requirements working, that should give you 3-4 marks which is pretty good.

Sample Answer

Question Breakdown & Tips and Tricks

Question: Write a SQL query that displays the contents of the Tasks table showing the taskName, status, dueDate and subjectName in ascending order of the dueDate. Only tasks that are due before 11-03-25 and are not done should be displayed. (3 marks)

Step 1. Read the question carefully

When reading the question, it's important to ask these two questions:

  • What is the topic/content area? Obviously this is an SQL question, but specifically it's testing your ability to select fields from multiple tables, how to use the WHERE clause on two fields and also ORDER the output. When practicing, you should always try to identify where the content is located in your syllabus so you can become more familiar with it and how it informs the questions you are asked. SQL is located throughout your programming for the web topic and specific information on the exact things you are required to know are on page 22 & 23 of your course specifications.
  • What are we required to do? We need to write an SQL query that shows the taskName, status, dueDate and subjectName which you should notice requires selecting data from multiple table. Is also specifies the ordering to be ascending by dueDate. The where clause will need two conditions so that only tasks that are due before 11-03-25 and not done are displayed.

Stimulus:

Step 2. Analyse the stimulus

In this question we would be glancing over to the stimulus as we read the question since the question contains most of the directive information we need to write the query. The stimulus is here only to show us the the layout of the database so we know what fields are in what table as we write each of the clauses in the query.

Before you move on, it might be useful for you to highlight all the parts of the query so you don't forget anything. You have three highlighter colours in the online HSC exam, so you could highlight the fields you need to SELECT in yellow, then you can highlight your conditions for the WHERE clause in red and the ORDER BY requirements in blue.

Step 3. Create and test your SQL query

Writing your Query: There are some simple steps you can follow while writing your query which will help ensure you don't miss anything important:

  1. Always start writing your SQL query by writing the SELECT clause by including the required fields you want to see in the output. At the same time, you should include the tables your fields come from in the FROM clause. Make sure you don't miss any by looking at your yellow highlights.
  2. Next, you should ensure you include all the required conditions in your WHERE clause by looking at your red highlights. These are red because they are important to get right. You should read them carefully to ensure you use the right logical operators. There's nothing worse than being off by one because you misread "tasks due before 11-03-25" as "tasks due up to 11-03-25" and used "<=" instead of "<". 
  3. Finally, you should complete your ORDER BY clause by looking at your blue highlights.

Testing your Query: To test your query, you can click the "Run" button which will be available in your exam environment. It will produce an output which you can inspect to ensure all the correct fields have been displayed and all rows satisfy the WHERE condition(s) and ORDER BY clause. If there is a syntax error in your query, you will be presented with an error that will show you where the error is at the very least and depending on the error even the type/cause of the error.

Step 4. Check your response is correct

For this question, we will quickly glance at our highlights again and ensure the output if the query is correct. You shouldn't need to check too much since after testing your query, it should be in working condition and correct.

 Marking Guidelines (from the perspective of a marker)

How do I get full marks?

  • To get full marks, you need to provide a completely correct SQL query. Ways you can ensure you get full marks in these types of questions are coming up with a criteria for the types of records you would expect to see in the output of your query. If you see records that aren't supposed to be there, or can see ones in the table that haven't appeared in the query output, you know the query must be wrong. Refine it until the output is perfect and when it is, you know you have a correct answer.
  • You need to be on top of your SQL query writing skills. To refresh your understanding and skills, revise 2.18 Web-Based Databases.

 I'm completely stuck. How do I maximise my marks?

  • Don't leave the question blank. If you're totally stuck, there are always some basic things you can do to guarantee at least one or two marks. After this, flag the question so you can come back to it after you finish the rest of the exam, hopefully with fresh ideas to claim a few more marks.
  •  You'll notice in the marking criteria that there is one mark for showing "some understanding of the problem". This means just writing the SELECT clause or maybe ORDER BY clause could get you one mark. This is why we don't leave a question blank since one mark is better than 0. To get two marks you need to provide a "substantially correct" query which means even if you make a few mistakes you could get two marks so long as you have both tables in your FROM clause. Don't give up and with a good attempt, you could get most of the marks.

Written Short Answer (Outline, Describe, Compare, Discuss, Explain, Justify, Analyse/Assess)

Unit3 Mastering the HSC Exam (Short Answer)

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Learn how to answer questions accurately and with the right level of detail for the number of marks.
  • Learn how to structure short answer responses based on the NESA key verb being used.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Apply their knowledge to answer short answer questions.
  • Structure their responses based on the NESA key verb.
  • Produce responses of the appropriate length for the question type and number of marks.

  Content

How to Answer "Short Answer" Questions

Procedure:

  1. Read the question carefully to identify the NESA key verb and topic area.
  2. Analyse any provided stimulus.
  3. Plan your response quickly in your head based on the NESA key verb and mark allocation.
  4. Write your response. Ensure you relate to the scenario/include examples.
  5. Re-read the question and make sure your answer meets the demands of the question.

 

Different Types of Short Answer Questions

Short answer questions can range in difficulty, expected length, and marks. Normally the difficultly of the key verb defines how many marks and how long your response needs to be. For example an identify question is normally 1-2 marks, and far easier to answer than an explain question which is normally 3-4 marks.

NESA Key Verbs You Need to Know

  • The NESA key verbs you are likely to encounter in your HSC Enterprise Computing HSC exam are listed below.
  • We will be looking at an example of each on this page so you can get an idea of how to structure your response since the key verb directly dictates the structure and content of your response. Without the correct structure you may not be able to get full marks, so it's important you understand and practice responses to different key verbs. 
  • You may sometimes find that two key verbs have been used in a single question. For example a recommend and justify question is a fusion of two higher end verbs which requires you to provides reasons in favour of why each recommendation answers the question. These fusion questions are often worth more marks and more structurally and cognitively complex.
Verb Band Description
Identify Band 1–3 Recognise and name.
Outline Band 1–3 Sketch in general terms; indicate the main features of.
Describe Band 2–4 Provide characteristics and features.
Compare Band 3–5 Show how things are similar or different.
Discuss Band 3–5 Identify issues and provide points for and/or against.
Recommend Band 3–5 Provide reasons in favour.

Explain

Why/How

 Band 4–6
  • Relate cause and effect.
  • Make the relationships between things evident.
  • Provide why and/or how.
Justify Band 4-6 Support an argument or conclusion.
Assess Band 5-6 Make a judgement of value, quality, outcomes, results or size.
Analyse Band 5-6
  • Identify components and the relationship between them.
  • Draw out and relate implications.

 

Common Mark Allocations & Expected Time Spent and Response Length

  • In the exam, you get roughly 1.8 minutes per mark, however you want to working slightly ahead of this if you can to ensure you have time for harder questions. This means you have about 5 minutes to complete a 3 mark question and about 9 minutes to complete a 5 mark question, etc. 
  • In the online exam environment there will be a word counter below of your answer text box and it will show something like "0/150 words", which shows you how many words you have written and how many words you are expected to write. Note that you are able to write more than the recommended number, there is no word limit. The word indicator will just start to show something like "183/150 words".
  • If you have the knowledge and time to write a little extra to include an "insurance policy" point, this is often a good idea so long as you stay within the time allocated for the question. However, it's not a good idea to write a lot less than the amount unless you are very succinct. A correctly structured response at the length specified is a recipe to get full marks.
Marks Max Time Allocation (1.8 mins per mark)  Time to aim for
1-2 1.8–3.6 mins 1-3 mins
3-4 5.4–7.2 mins 5-7 mins
5-6 9–10.8 mins 8-10 mins
7-8 12.6–14.4 mins 12-14 mins

Note that you should be aiming to complete question in slightly less time that in the table since some harder questions may require more time so you want to have a little time to spare at the end so you can go back to questions you flagged and develop more complex answers further. Use this table as a guide for the maximum time to spend on each question, but don't hesitate to work faster as long as you are confident. It's also important not to rush. Give each question it's due attention and love.

How to Get Full Marks in Short Answer Questions

  • Relate to the scenario and give examples. If there is a provided stimulus, you must engage with it by responding to ideas/requirements it imposes. If there is no stimulus, you still need to come back to the terms of the question and use examples which relate to the topic and requirements of the question. You are aiming to write an answer that is tailor made for the question and wouldn't fit any other. This shows that you've truly understood the question and will make it easier for the marker to pay you marks.
  • Structure your response appropriately. Make sure you structure your response appropriately for the NESA verb and number of marks. Each verb has a very specific type of response it wants you to engage in and if you don't follow this structure you can loose one or more marks. The examples below will take you through how to structure your response for each of the most common NESA verbs.
  • Know your content — You need to be on top of your content so that you can add accurate detail to the body of your answers. Structuring the response is the first and most important thing, but then the actual substance of the response that sits in the frame of the NESA verb will come from your understanding of the course content. Your examples/relation to the scenario will be added in addition to your content recall to bolster your response and prove you actually understand it.

Answer Structure

  1. Brief topic sentence or phrase that addresses the question.
  2. Body of your response which sketches each of your points in general terms.

Question Breakdown & Tips and Tricks

Question: Outline the difference between artificial intelligence and machine learning. (2 marks)

Step 1. Read the Question Carefully.

When reading a question, it's important to ask these two questions

  1. What is the topic/content area? This question is testing your knowledge of machine learning and artificial intelligence. Specifically it's testing the dot point "Distinguish between artificial intelligence (AI) and ML" in your software automation topic. Revise 3.2 Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, if required
  2. What are we required to do? Highlight the NESA key verb in red so you don't forget it. We are required to outline the difference between artificial intelligence and machine learning. This means we need to sketch in general terms what distinguishes them.

There is no stimulus for this question so we will skip step 2.

Step 3. Plan your response quickly in your head.

Since this is a 2 mark outline question we don't need too much content. We will start by outlining what AI is and then outline what machine learning is and how it differs from AI.

Step 4. Write your response

  • For an outline you just need to sketch in general terms each of your points so we will only write a sentence or two for each point.
  • Relate to the Scenario/Question. Even though this is a simple question we will need to adhere to the golden rule "relate to the scenario/question". This means you should use terms from the question throughout your response. Below, the links back to the question have been highlighted in purple. 
  • Give clear examples. When there is no explicit scenario, it's important to give examples to enhance the clarity and nuance of your answer. Since this is an outline question, you don't need to go into too much detail.

Sample Answer Analysis: Artificial intelligence is the technology or concept that involves machines simulating human intelligence to perform analog, variable, reasoning, decision-making, and problem-solving tasks. Machine learning is the process by which artificial intelligence is created and trained. It focuses on training algorithms to allow computers to learn patterns from data and improve their performance without explicit programming. AI is the end result of machine learning.

Step 5. Check your response is correct

Quickly reread the question and try highlighting your response in your head if you're in an exam or in a word processor if you are practicing. Make sure there is enough purple and blue and also some green and yellow.

  1. We have sketched both artificial intelligence and machine learning in general terms and how they differ.

Marking Criteria (through the eyes of a marker)

How do I get full marks?

  • Structure your response appropriately. To get full marks you just need to outline the difference between artificial intelligence and machine learning.
  • Know your content — You need to be on top of your ML and AI content. Revise 3.2 Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning.

I'm completely stuck. How do I maximise my marks?

  • Don't leave the question blank. If you're totally stuck, there are always some basic things you can do to guarantee at least one or two marks. After this, flag the question so you can come back to it after you finish the rest of the exam, hopefully with fresh ideas to claim a few more marks.
  • As per the marking criteria, if you don't know how to outline both and show the difference, you could also just identify a difference without outlining it or outlining what machine learning or artificial intelligence is without their differences. If you're about to run out of time, you can also just write something you think is relevant and it may end up being correct.

Describe

Describe Questions

NESA Definition — Describe

Provide characteristics and features.

Answer Structure

  1. Brief topic sentence or phrase that addresses the question.
  2. Body of your response that provides characteristics and features of what you are describing. You should aim to provide enough characteristics/features so that you produce a well rounded description. This is normally 2-3.

Question Breakdown & Tips and Tricks

Question: Describe TWO different types of machine learning models and their uses. (3 marks)

Step 1. Read the Question Carefully.

When reading a question, it's important to ask these two questions

  1. What is the topic/content area? This question is testing your knowledge of machine learning training models. This is under the "Explore models of training ML" dot point of your software automation topic. Revise 3.3 ML Training Models, if needed.
  2. What are we required to do? Highlight the NESA key verb in red so you don't forget it. We are required to describe two different types of machine learning models and their uses. This means we need to provide characteristics and features of these models and gives examples of how they are used.

There is no stimulus for this question so we will skip step 2.

Step 3. Plan your response quickly in your head.

In your head take a mental note of the two things you are required to do which are providing the characteristics of two ML training models of your choice. There are four, pick the two you are most confident with.

Step 4. Write your response

  • Use the correct structure: Make sure you follow the describe structure. This involves providing characteristics and features for each of your points.
    • Brief topic sentence.
    • Characteristics and features of your points.
  • Relate to the Scenario/Question. This means you should use terms from the question throughout your response, make links back to the ideas/context given in the question, and draw from the stimulus. Below, the links back to the question have been highlighted in purple. 
  • Give clear examples. When there is no explicit scenario, it's important to give examples to enhance the clarity and nuance of answer. In this describe question, giving examples is an extremely powerful way to elevate your description and prove to the marker you know what you are talking about.
  • Know your content. It's important to think about where this question comes from in your syllabus as you read the question, recall what you have learned about that topic and then include as much relevant information as you can to flesh out your answer.

 Sample Answer Analysis: Machine learning models are categorised into four main types based on the type of data and learning process. The most common is supervised learning, which uses labelled data, so the algorithm learns to map inputs to the correct outputs. When it encounters new, unseen data, it can make accurate predictions based on the learned relationships, making it useful for applications like spam detection and language translation. Another model type, Reinforcement learning, involves training a model through interactions with an environment. The model, often called an agent, learns by receiving feedback in the form of rewards or penalties based on the actions it takes. This makes it useful for developing models for autonomous vehicles and robotics.

Step 5. Check your response is correct

Quickly reread the question and try highlighting your response in your head if you're in an exam or in a word processor if you are practicing. Make sure there is enough purple and blue and plenty of yellow.

  1. We have two clear descriptions following a clear topic sentence which identifies what we are going to expand on.
  2. There is not really much context or stimulus for this question, so instead of relating back to the scenario, we've included examples that relate to what we are describing.

 Marking Criteria (through the eyes of a marker)

 

How do I get full marks?

  • Structure your response appropriately. To get full marks you just need to describe TWO machine learning models and their uses.
  • Know your content — You need to be on top of your ML Training model content. Revise 3.3 ML Training Models.

I'm completely stuck. How do I maximise my marks?

  • Don't leave the question blank. If you're totally stuck, there are always some basic things you can do to guarantee at least one or two marks. After this, flag the question so you can come back to it after you finish the rest of the exam, hopefully with fresh ideas to claim a few more marks.
  • As per the marking criteria, you can get one mark for providing "some relevant information".  Always put something down even if you don't think it's correct since you won't have marks taken away for doing something wrong, you only gain marks for doing things right.

Compare

Compare Questions

NESA Definition — Compare

Show how things are similar or different.

Answer Structure

  1. Brief topic sentence or phrase that addresses the question.
  2. For compare question, you need to mention both similarities and differences. In total, you need to have the number of marks minus one similarities + differences, so for a four mark question, you are aiming for one difference and two similarities or two differences and one similarity.

Sample Answer

Question Breakdown & Tips and Tricks

Question: Compare server-side and client-side web programming. (4 marks)

Step 1. Read the Question Carefully.

When reading a question, it's important to ask these two questions

  1. What is the topic/content area? This question is testing your knowledge of server-side and client-side web programming. This is under the "Model elements that form a web development system" dot point of your programming for the web topic. Revise 2.7 Web Elements, if required.
  2. What are we required to do? Highlight the NESA key verb in red so you don't forget it. We are required to compare server-side and client-side web programming, which means we need to outline/describe the similarities and differences between the two.

 There is no stimulus for this question so we will skip step 2.

Step 3. Plan your response quickly in your head.

In your head, take a mental note of the two things you are required to do which are describing the similarities and differences of server-side and client-side web programming. They have more differences than similarities. The one similarity is that they are both used for building dynamic and functional website, so we will get that out of the way to begin with so we don't forget and then go into at least two differences.

Step 4. Write your response

  • Use the correct structure: Make sure you follow the compare structure. This involves providing similarities and differences.
    • Start with a topic sentence which includes the phrase "many similarities and differences" which signposts to the marker you are going to write a response in the correct format and tells them exactly what is in your question so they can give you marks with minimal friction.
    • Use text connectives between your points. When transitioning between similarities and differences, you can use a word such as "conversely" to signpost to the marker that you are beginning your the next section of your response. Between points of the same side, you can use connectives like "additionally" and "furthermore" to indicate the the separation of your points, making it easy for the marker to give you marks.
  • Relate to the Scenario/Question. Never forget the golden rule "relate to the scenario/question". This means you should use terms from the question throughout your response make links back to the ideas/context given in the question. Below, the links back to the question have been highlighted in purple. 
  • Give clear examples. Give examples for extra clarity and to show a detailed, nuanced understanding of a concept. They have not explicitly asked for examples in the question, we but are going to include them anyway since HSC markers expect them. You can also use examples to relate back to the scenario. Below, examples are highlighted in blue.
  • Know your content. It's important to think about where this question comes from in your syllabus as you read the question, recall what you have learned about that topic and then include as much relevant information as you can to flesh out your answer.

Sample Answer Analysis: There are many similarities and differences between server-side and client-side web programming. A similarity is that they are both used to develop responsive and functional web pages that are secure and reliable; however, despite their interdependence, they are fundamentally different things. Firstly, client-side programming is executed in the user's browser, with a focus on the user interface, instant feedback, and interactivity. It employs technologies such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Conversely, server-side programming is executed on the web server and handles more complex back-end logic, such as database queries and authentication. It employs languages like PHP, Python, Node.js. Moreover, client-side code is exposed to the user, while server-side code is not.

Step 5. Check your response is correct

Quickly reread the question and try highlighting your response in your head if you're in an exam or in a word processor if you are practicing. Make sure there is enough purple and blue and also some green and yellow.

  1. Here we have described enough similarities and differences, and we've structured the response in a cohesive and logical way which makes it very easy for the marker to see and differentiate our points and consequently award marks.
  2. Since there is no clear scenario or context, we've included some examples. Even though the question didn't specify this, we did it any way since it's what HSC markers expect.

Marking Criteria (through the eyes of a marker)


How do I get full marks?

  • Relate to the scenario and give examples. In the marking criteria, to get full marks, you must provide at least 1 similarity and two differences between client-side and sever-side programming. To provide a similarity, you need to describe a common element between the two and for differences, you need to describe something that differs between the two.
  • Structure your response appropriately. A compare question requires similarities and differences. If you forget the similarities you could get as low as 2 or maybe 3 if your differences are really good. 
  • Know your content — You need to be on top of your web programming content. Revise 2.7 Web Elements.

I'm completely stuck. How do I maximise my marks?

  • Don't leave the question blank. If you're totally stuck, there are always some basic things you can do to guarantee at least one or two marks. After this, flag the question so you can come back to it after you finish the rest of the exam, hopefully with fresh ideas to claim a few more marks.
  • In this question, providing some relevant information will get you one mark. This could be as simple as attempting to explain what client-side or server-side programming is. The next step up is listing similarities or differences and to get three marks you just need to describe a single similarity and difference.

 

Discuss

Discuss Questions

NESA Definition — Discuss

Identify issues and provide points for and/or against.

Answer Structure

  1. Brief topic sentence or phrase that addresses the question.
  2. For compare questions, you need to mention both positives and negatives of a given discussion subject. Most describe questions are 3-4 marks, so are are aiming for 3-4 similarities + differences, commonly split as two similarities followed by two differences.
